questions.title: ROW_NUMBER vs. RANK vs. DENSE_RANK
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() in SQL Server. If two products are tied for the highest price, what number does each function give the row right after them?
questions.modelAnswer: All three are ranking window functions used with OVER(ORDER BY ...), and all three number rows based on the order you specify, but they disagree on what happens with ties. ROW_NUMBER() always assigns a unique, sequential integer to every row, even when two rows are tied on the ORDER BY column -- one of the tied rows arbitrarily gets the lower number. RANK() gives tied rows the same number, but then skips ahead by the size of the tie: if two rows tie for rank 1, the next distinct row gets rank 3, not 2, because RANK() is really counting 'how many rows came before or tied with me, plus one.' DENSE_RANK() also gives tied rows the same number, but the next distinct value gets the very next integer with no gap -- it's counting distinct values, not rows. So for two products tied for the most expensive: ROW_NUMBER gives them 1 and 2 (arbitrarily), RANK gives them both 1 and the next product gets 3, and DENSE_RANK gives them both 1 and the next product gets 2.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it with a concrete example because the difference only shows up when there's a tie. Say I'm ranking products by ListPrice and two products are tied for the top price. ROW_NUMBER() doesn't know about ties at all -- it just hands out 1, 2, 3, 4 in order, so the two tied products arbitrarily get 1 and 2. RANK() respects the tie -- both get rank 1 -- but it still 'reserves' a slot for each of them, so the next product down is rank 3, not 2. DENSE_RANK() is the one that feels most natural for something like a pricing tier: both tied products get 1, and the next distinct price is simply 2, no gap. In practice I reach for ROW_NUMBER() constantly for deduplication -- partition by the natural key, order by something like an ID, and anything with RowNum greater than 1 is a duplicate I can delete. I reach for RANK() when ties should genuinely cost a position, like a sales leaderboard where two reps tied for 2nd really does mean nobody is 3rd. And I reach for DENSE_RANK() when I just want the next distinct tier number and don't want gaps confusing anyone reading the report.
questions.example:
SELECT Name, ListPrice,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS RowNum,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS Rank_,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS DenseRank_
FROM Production.Product
ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
-- If two products tie for the top ListPrice:
-- RowNum:     1, 2, 3, 4...  (ties broken arbitrarily)
-- Rank_:      1, 1, 3, 4...  (skips to 3 after the tie)
-- DenseRank_: 1, 1, 2, 3...  (no gap after the tie)
commonMistakes: Saying ROW_NUMBER() can produce duplicate numbers for ties (it never can -- it's always unique)
Mixing up which function skips numbers after a tie (it's RANK, not DENSE_RANK)
Forgetting that ROW_NUMBER() requires ORDER BY inside OVER() -- without it, row order is undefined
Not realizing all three still need PARTITION BY to restart numbering per group
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER() always produces unique numbers, ties broken arbitrarily
RANK() gives ties the same number and skips ahead by the tie size afterward
DENSE_RANK() gives ties the same number with no gap for the next distinct value
Choice depends on whether the business question treats a tie as 'costing' a rank

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes ROW_NUMBER's uniqueness behavior
Correctly describes RANK's gap-after-tie behavior
Correctly describes DENSE_RANK's no-gap behavior
Gives a realistic scenario for choosing one over another

questions.title: Transactions: BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK
questions.prompt: Explain what a transaction is in SQL Server, what COMMIT does that running the statements without a transaction wouldn't, and what exactly ROLLBACK undoes.
questions.modelAnswer: A transaction groups one or more statements into a single all-or-nothing unit. BEGIN TRANSACTION marks the start of that group. Until COMMIT runs, the changes are provisional -- visible in the current session but not yet permanently saved, and still subject to being undone. COMMIT TRANSACTION makes every change inside the group permanent, all at once. ROLLBACK TRANSACTION undoes every change made since the matching BEGIN TRANSACTION, as if none of it had ever happened. The reason this matters: a multi-step change (like moving stock from one location to another with two separate UPDATE statements) can fail halfway through if run as two independent statements, leaving the data in an inconsistent state. Wrapping both statements in a transaction guarantees either both succeed or neither does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I usually explain this with the classic example: moving inventory from warehouse A to warehouse B is really two UPDATEs -- subtract from A, add to B. If I just run those as two separate statements and the second one fails, I've got stock that's vanished into nowhere. A transaction fixes that by treating both statements as one all-or-nothing unit. BEGIN TRANSACTION starts the clock; until I COMMIT, those changes are provisional -- I can see them in my own session, but they're not durably saved and SQL Server can still throw them away. COMMIT makes them permanent. ROLLBACK is the safety net -- if something goes wrong partway through, it undoes everything back to the BEGIN, cleanly, as if I'd never run anything at all. The discipline I bring to it professionally is keeping transactions as short as possible, because every lock held inside one is held until COMMIT or ROLLBACK runs.
commonMistakes: Thinking changes inside a transaction are already permanent before COMMIT runs
Forgetting that ROLLBACK undoes everything since BEGIN TRANSACTION, not just the most recent statement
Leaving a transaction open for a long time, holding locks and blocking other users unnecessarily
Not pairing every BEGIN TRANSACTION with a guaranteed COMMIT or ROLLBACK, even on the error path
keyPoints: A transaction is an all-or-nothing group of statements
Changes are provisional until COMMIT makes them permanent
ROLLBACK undoes everything since the matching BEGIN TRANSACTION
Transactions exist to prevent partial, inconsistent multi-step changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a transaction groups together
Correctly explains what COMMIT does and the provisional state before it
Correctly explains the scope of what ROLLBACK undoes
Gives a realistic scenario showing why this matters

questions.title: EXISTS vs. IN vs. JOIN for Existence Checks
questions.prompt: You need to find every customer who has placed at least one order. Compare writing this with EXISTS, with IN, and with an INNER JOIN plus DISTINCT. Explain how each one behaves when a customer has multiple orders, and the specific trap with NOT IN when the subquery's column can contain NULLs.
questions.modelAnswer: EXISTS, IN, and INNER JOIN with DISTINCT can all answer 'does this customer have at least one order,' but they get there differently. EXISTS(subquery) is a pure existence check -- SQL Server can stop scanning the moment it finds one matching row, and a customer with ten orders still only produces one result row, because EXISTS never actually returns the subquery's rows, just a true/false per outer row. IN (subquery) compares the outer column against the whole list the subquery returns; it also naturally avoids duplication since it's testing membership, not joining. An INNER JOIN behaves differently: joining Customer to Order on CustomerID and a customer with three orders produces three joined rows, which means DISTINCT (or GROUP BY) is required afterward to get back to one row per customer -- without it, the result silently overcounts. The sharper trap is with NOT IN rather than IN: if the subquery's column can contain a NULL, NOT IN against that list returns no rows at all for every single outer row, because SQL's three-valued logic can never prove an inequality against an unknown value. EXISTS doesn't have this problem because it's testing a condition, not comparing against a value list, which is one reason NOT EXISTS is generally the safer choice for 'does not have a match.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through why these three roads to the same destination aren't actually equivalent in practice. EXISTS is the one I reach for by default for a pure existence check -- it's a yes/no test, the optimizer can bail out the instant it finds one match, and a customer with ten orders still contributes exactly one row to the result, because EXISTS never pulls the subquery's actual data back. IN behaves similarly for this particular case -- it's checking membership in a list, not joining, so it also doesn't duplicate. Where people get burned is reaching for a plain INNER JOIN instead: the moment you join Customer to Order, a customer with three orders becomes three rows, and if you forget the DISTINCT, you've silently inflated your result set without an error anywhere to tell you. But the real gotcha I always bring up, because it's bitten people in production, is NOT IN with a nullable column -- if even one NULL sneaks into the subquery's result, NOT IN returns completely empty, for every row, with no warning. I treat that as a hard rule: never write NOT IN against a column that could contain NULL -- use NOT EXISTS instead, which doesn't have that failure mode at all.
questions.example:
-- EXISTS: pure existence check, no duplication risk
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM [Order] o WHERE o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID);

-- IN: membership test against the subquery's result list
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
WHERE c.CustomerID IN (SELECT o.CustomerID FROM [Order] o);

-- JOIN: requires DISTINCT or a customer with 3 orders appears 3 times
SELECT DISTINCT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
INNER JOIN [Order] o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID;

-- THE TRAP: if Order.CustomerID can be NULL, this returns ZERO rows for every customer:
SELECT c.CustomerID FROM Customer c
WHERE c.CustomerID NOT IN (SELECT o.CustomerID FROM [Order] o); -- avoid if nullable
commonMistakes: Writing a plain INNER JOIN for an existence check and forgetting DISTINCT, silently duplicating customers with multiple orders
Using NOT IN against a subquery column that can contain NULL, not realizing it returns zero rows for every outer row
Assuming EXISTS and IN always perform identically to a JOIN, when EXISTS can short-circuit and avoid materializing the whole list
Not recognizing that EXISTS never actually returns the subquery's column values -- only whether a match exists
keyPoints: EXISTS is a short-circuiting existence check; it returns one result row regardless of how many matches exist
IN compares against a list but doesn't duplicate rows the way a JOIN does
An INNER JOIN needs DISTINCT/GROUP BY to avoid duplicating a row per matching child record
NOT IN against a nullable column can return zero rows entirely -- NOT EXISTS avoids that trap

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains EXISTS's existence-check, non-duplicating behavior
Correctly explains why a JOIN needs DISTINCT to avoid duplication
Correctly identifies the NOT IN / NULL trap and why NOT EXISTS avoids it
Provides correct, illustrative SQL for at least two of the three approaches

questions.title: CTEs vs. Views: Same Shape, Different Lifetime
questions.prompt: A coworker says, "I don't get why we need views — a CTE already lets me name a subquery." Explain the real difference between a CTE and a view, and when you'd reach for one over the other.
questions.modelAnswer: A CTE and a view can look nearly identical — both let you name a SELECT and reference it like a table — but they differ in lifetime and scope. A CTE, defined with WITH, exists only for the single statement immediately following it; the moment that statement finishes, the CTE is gone, and no other query, session, or user can reference it. A view, created with CREATE VIEW, is a permanent database object: it's saved once and can be queried by name from any session, any user with permission, indefinitely, until someone runs DROP VIEW. Neither one stores actual data — both re-run their underlying SELECT against live data every time they're referenced. The practical rule: reach for a CTE to make one complex query more readable, especially when you need to reference the same intermediate result twice in that query. Reach for a view when the same logic needs to be reused across many different queries, by many different people or tools, including reporting tools like Power BI connecting directly to the database.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with the one-sentence version first: a CTE lives for one statement, a view lives forever until someone deletes it. If I'm writing a gnarly query with three levels of nested subqueries and I just want to name the middle layer so I can read my own logic back, that's a CTE — it's disposable, scoped to right here, right now. But if I've built a 'active customers with more than $1,000 in lifetime orders' query that three different reports are going to need, I don't want three copies of that logic drifting out of sync — I'd save it once as a view, under a clear name, so every query and every person on the team references the same definition. I'd also mention that a view is a real object other tools can see too — if Power BI is connecting directly to the database instead of importing through Power Query, it can query a view exactly like a table, which a CTE could never support.
questions.example:
-- CTE: scoped to this one statement only
WITH RecentOrders AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, SUM(TotalDue) AS Total
    FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
    WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01'
    GROUP BY CustomerID
)
SELECT * FROM RecentOrders WHERE Total > 5000;
-- RecentOrders no longer exists after this statement runs.

-- View: saved permanently, reusable by anyone with access
CREATE VIEW vw_RecentOrderTotals AS
SELECT CustomerID, SUM(TotalDue) AS Total
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01'
GROUP BY CustomerID;

SELECT * FROM vw_RecentOrderTotals WHERE Total > 5000;
commonMistakes: Assuming a CTE can be reused across multiple separate statements or sessions (it can't)
Assuming either one stores a physical copy of the data (both re-run their SELECT live)
Reaching for a view for a one-off readability fix inside a single complex query, when a CTE is simpler and doesn't leave a permanent object behind
Forgetting that a view is directly queryable by reporting tools connecting to the database, the way a CTE never could be
keyPoints: A CTE is scoped to one statement; a view persists until explicitly dropped
Neither stores data — both run their SELECT fresh against live data each time
CTEs suit one-off readability inside a single complex query
Views suit logic that needs to be reused across many queries, people, or tools

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains a CTE's one-statement lifetime
Correctly explains a view's persistent, reusable lifetime
States that neither stores data, both re-run live
Gives a realistic scenario for choosing one over the other

questions.title: What Makes a Window Function Different from GROUP BY
questions.prompt: Explain how a window function using OVER() differs from GROUP BY, and why you might reach for AVG(Price) OVER (PARTITION BY Category) instead of a GROUP BY query, even though both compute an average per category.
questions.modelAnswer: GROUP BY and a window function can compute the exact same aggregate — an average per category — but they do fundamentally different things to the result set. GROUP BY collapses every row in a group down into a single summary row, so a table of 500 products grouped by category becomes a handful of rows, one per category, with the individual products gone. A window function, triggered by adding OVER() to an aggregate, computes the same aggregate across a group of related rows but keeps every original row intact in the output — nothing collapses. PARTITION BY inside OVER() divides rows into groups purely for that calculation's purpose, exactly like GROUP BY divides rows, but the row-level result is untouched. The practical reason to reach for the window function version: you need the category average sitting alongside each individual product's own price, for example to compute how far above or below that category's average a specific product is priced — a comparison GROUP BY's collapsed output couldn't support at all, since the individual product's own price no longer exists in a grouped result.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start with what actually happens to the rows, because that's the real distinction, not just syntax. GROUP BY by category gives me one row per category — Bikes, Accessories, Clothing — and the individual products are gone from the output. AVG(Price) OVER (PARTITION BY Category) gives me back every single product row, but now each one also carries its own category's average price as an extra column sitting right next to it. That's the whole reason I'd reach for the window function version: I usually want to compare something at the row level against a group-level number — 'how does this specific product's price compare to the average for its category?' — and I can only do that math if both numbers are available on the same row. If all I actually need is the category averages themselves, with no individual rows attached, plain GROUP BY is simpler and I wouldn't bother with OVER() at all.
questions.example:
-- GROUP BY: collapses to one row per category
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, AVG(ListPrice) AS AvgPrice
FROM Production.Product
GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID;

-- Window function: keeps every product row, adds the category average alongside it
SELECT Name, ProductSubcategoryID, ListPrice,
       AVG(ListPrice) OVER (PARTITION BY ProductSubcategoryID) AS AvgPriceForCategory,
       ListPrice - AVG(ListPrice) OVER (PARTITION BY ProductSubcategoryID) AS DiffFromAvg
FROM Production.Product;
commonMistakes: Saying GROUP BY and a window function always return the same number of rows (GROUP BY collapses; a window function does not)
Forgetting PARTITION BY is required to restart the calculation per group, not just ORDER BY
Assuming a window function requires an aggregate you can't also compute with GROUP BY — the aggregate itself is identical, only the row-collapsing behavior differs
Using GROUP BY when the goal was actually a row-level comparison against a group total, then wondering why the individual values disappeared
keyPoints: GROUP BY collapses rows into one summary row per group
A window function (OVER()) keeps every original row while still computing a per-group aggregate
PARTITION BY divides rows into groups for the window calculation only, without collapsing anything
Choose the window function when you need a row-level value compared against a group-level aggregate

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains GROUP BY's row-collapsing behavior
Correctly explains that a window function preserves every row
Correctly describes PARTITION BY's role
Gives a realistic scenario where the window function's row-level detail matters

questions.title: Null Hypothesis, Alternative Hypothesis, and What a p-Value Actually Measures
questions.prompt: Explain what the null hypothesis and alternative hypothesis represent in a hypothesis test, and explain precisely what a p-value is measuring. What's wrong with saying 'the p-value is the probability the null hypothesis is true'?
questions.modelAnswer: The null hypothesis (H0) is the default, no-effect claim -- for example, 'this new checkout flow has no effect on conversion rate.' The alternative hypothesis (H1) is the claim you're actually trying to find evidence for -- 'the new checkout flow changes conversion rate.' A hypothesis test doesn't prove either one; it asks how surprising the data you actually observed would be if the null hypothesis were true. That's exactly what a p-value measures: the probability of seeing a result at least as extreme as what you observed, assuming the null hypothesis is correct. It is NOT the probability that the null hypothesis itself is true -- that's a common and serious misreading. A p-value is a statement about the data given the null hypothesis, not a statement about the null hypothesis given the data; those are different conditional probabilities, and confusing them is one of the most common statistical errors in practice.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd anchor this in a concrete example rather than abstract definitions. Say I'm testing whether a new checkout flow changes conversion rate. My null hypothesis is the boring, no-effect claim: there's no real difference, and whatever gap I see in the data is just random noise. My alternative hypothesis is the claim I'm hoping to support: there really is a difference. Running the test and getting a p-value of 0.03 does not mean there's a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true -- that's the single most common misstatement I hear, and it's wrong. What it actually means is: if the null hypothesis were true and there really were no effect, I'd see a gap this large or larger only 3% of the time just from random sampling noise. That's a statement about how surprising my data is under an assumption, not a verdict on whether the assumption is correct. I'm careful to phrase it that way out loud specifically because stakeholders reach for the wrong interpretation by default, and it's my job to correct that, not reinforce it.
commonMistakes: Saying the p-value is the probability the null hypothesis is true (it's the probability of the data, assuming H0 is true, not the reverse)
Treating the alternative hypothesis as something the test 'proves' rather than something evidence accumulates toward
Forgetting that a hypothesis test never actually confirms H0 -- failing to reject it just means insufficient evidence against it
Not stating the null hypothesis in a specific, testable way before running any test
keyPoints: H0 is the no-effect default claim; H1 is the effect being tested for
A p-value is P(data this extreme | H0 is true), not P(H0 is true | data)
The test never proves H0 true -- it only measures evidence against it
Confusing the two conditional probabilities is a well-known, serious statistical error

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines the null and alternative hypotheses with a concrete example
Correctly and precisely defines what a p-value measures
Explicitly identifies and corrects the 'probability H0 is true' misreading
Notes a test never proves the null hypothesis true

questions.title: What a 95% Confidence Interval Actually Means
questions.prompt: A colleague says, 'our 95% confidence interval for average order value is $42 to $48, so there's a 95% chance the true average is in that range.' Is that correct? Explain what a 95% confidence interval actually means.
questions.modelAnswer: That phrasing is a very common but technically incorrect interpretation. The true population average order value is a fixed, unknown number -- it either is or isn't in the $42-$48 range, so it doesn't make sense to assign a 95% probability to something that isn't random. What 95% confidence actually describes is the long-run reliability of the procedure used to build the interval: if you repeated this same sampling process many times and built a new confidence interval from each sample, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true population average. The confidence level is a property of the method across repeated samples, not a probability statement about this one specific interval. In practice, the practical takeaway is still useful -- a narrower interval generally means a more precise estimate -- but the 'probability the true value is in here' phrasing should be avoided in anything written for stakeholders.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd gently correct the phrasing, because this exact misreading comes up constantly and it's worth getting right. The true average order value is a single fixed number out there -- we just don't know it. It's already either inside $42-$48 or it isn't; there's no remaining randomness to assign a 95% probability to once the interval is calculated. What's actually random is the sampling process that produced this particular interval. The honest statement is: if we ran this same study over and over, drawing a new sample each time and building a new interval each time, about 95% of those intervals would end up containing the true average. This one interval is just one draw from that process -- it either worked or it didn't, and we can't know which from the interval alone. I usually tell stakeholders it's safer to think of the confidence level as describing how trustworthy the method is, not as a probability attached to this specific range.
commonMistakes: Saying there's a 95% probability the true value falls within this specific interval
Treating the confidence level as a property of the single computed interval rather than the sampling procedure
Assuming a narrower interval always means a more 'confident' result rather than a more precise one from the same confidence level
Conflating confidence intervals with prediction intervals, which have a different meaning
keyPoints: The true population parameter is fixed, not random -- it's already in the interval or it isn't
95% confidence describes the long-run reliability of the method across repeated sampling
It is not a probability statement about this one specific computed interval
Practical usefulness (precision via interval width) is still valid even with the correct interpretation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the colleague's statement as a common misinterpretation
Correctly explains the long-run, repeated-sampling meaning of confidence level
Explains why the true parameter isn't treated as random
Communicates this clearly enough for a non-technical colleague

questions.title: Correlation vs. Causation, With a Concrete Confounder
questions.prompt: Ice cream sales and drowning incidents are strongly positively correlated across months. Explain why this doesn't mean ice cream causes drowning, name the actual mechanism at work, and describe one thing you'd check in a real dataset before trusting any correlation as causal.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong correlation only tells you two variables tend to move together -- it says nothing about why. In this example, both ice cream sales and drowning incidents are driven by a third variable neither causes: warmer weather. When it's hot, more people buy ice cream and more people swim, which raises both ice cream sales and drowning risk simultaneously, with no causal link between the two directly. That third variable is called a confounder -- a factor that influences both variables being compared and creates an apparent relationship between them that isn't real. Before trusting any correlation as causal in a real dataset, I'd specifically look for plausible confounders -- is there some other variable (seasonality, a shared driver, a common cause) that could independently explain both sides of the relationship? Beyond that, a true causal claim really needs either a designed experiment (like an A/B test with random assignment) or a strong theoretical mechanism plus careful controls for known confounders -- correlation from observational data alone is never sufficient.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd use the classic version of this example because it makes the mechanism obvious: temperature is the hidden variable doing all the real work here. Hot weather makes people buy more ice cream, and separately, hot weather makes more people go swimming, which increases drowning risk. Ice cream and drowning end up correlated purely because they share a common cause, not because one causes the other. That's a confounder, and spotting it is really the whole skill behind 'correlation isn't causation' -- it's not just a slogan, it's a specific habit of asking 'is there some other variable that could independently be driving both of these?' before I get excited about a correlation I find in real data. In practice, before I'd ever present a correlation as if it were causal, I'd go looking for obvious confounders specific to that dataset, check whether the relationship holds up when I control for them, and ultimately remember that observational correlation alone, no matter how strong, isn't proof of a causal mechanism -- that really requires a controlled experiment or a much more rigorous causal-inference approach.
questions.example:
Correlation observed: corr(ice_cream_sales, drownings) = 0.82 across months.
Confounder: avg_monthly_temperature drives both.
Check: does the correlation shrink dramatically once you control for / stratify by temperature? If so, that confirms temperature (not ice cream) is the real driver.
commonMistakes: Concluding a causal relationship directly from a strong correlation coefficient
Not naming the actual confounding variable, leaving the explanation vague
Assuming controlling for one plausible confounder is sufficient proof of causation, rather than just reducing one alternative explanation
Forgetting that a true causal claim generally needs a controlled experiment, not just careful observational analysis
keyPoints: Correlation measures co-movement, not cause
A confounder (here, temperature) can independently drive both variables, creating a spurious correlation
Checking for plausible confounders is the practical first step before trusting any correlation
Real causal claims generally require a controlled experiment or rigorous causal-inference methods, not correlation alone

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why correlation doesn't imply causation here
Correctly identifies temperature as the specific confounder
Describes a concrete check for confounders in a real dataset
Notes what would actually be needed to support a causal claim

questions.title: merge, join, and concat in pandas
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between pandas' merge(), DataFrame.join(), and concat(). When would an inner merge silently drop rows you expected to keep, and how would you catch that before it causes a downstream reporting bug?
questions.modelAnswer: merge() combines two DataFrames based on matching values in one or more key columns, similar to a SQL join, and supports how='inner'/'left'/'right'/'outer'. join() is really a convenience wrapper around merge() that combines DataFrames based on their index by default, rather than an arbitrary column -- useful when the key is already the index. concat() is different in kind: it stacks DataFrames together along an axis (rows by default) without matching on any key at all -- it's really for appending similar-shaped data together, not relating two different datasets. The dangerous case is an inner merge: by default, merge() uses how='inner', which keeps only rows where the key exists in both DataFrames and silently drops every row whose key has no match on the other side -- no warning, no error, the row count just shrinks. To catch this before it causes a downstream bug, compare row counts before and after the merge (or check len(df) against the expected count), and inspect specifically which keys failed to match -- for example, using an outer merge with indicator=True temporarily to see the left_only/right_only/both breakdown.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of these as three different tools for three different jobs. concat() is the simplest -- it just stacks DataFrames on top of each other (or side by side), with no concept of matching keys at all; I use it to combine files with the same columns, like monthly exports. merge() is the real workhorse -- it's pandas' version of a SQL join, matching rows based on key column values, and I always have to consciously choose how='inner'/'left'/'outer' because that choice decides what happens to unmatched rows. join() is basically merge() but defaulting to the DataFrame's index as the key, which is convenient but easy to forget is happening. The bug I've actually been burned by is the default how='inner' on merge() quietly dropping orders whose customer_id didn't exist in the customers table -- the merged DataFrame just came out smaller, with zero errors, and I didn't notice until a revenue total didn't match. Since then, my habit is to check len() before and after every merge, and if the row count drops unexpectedly, run the same merge with how='outer' and indicator=True so I can actually see which keys are left_only or right_only and go figure out why.
questions.example:
merged = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left")
print(len(orders), len(merged))  # should match for a left merge

# Debugging an unexpected row-count drop:
check = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="outer", indicator=True)
print(check["_merge"].value_counts())  # left_only / right_only / both
commonMistakes: Assuming merge() always preserves every row from the left DataFrame, forgetting the default is how='inner'
Using concat() when the data actually needs to be matched on a key, producing misaligned rows
Not checking row counts before/after a merge, letting silent data loss reach a report undetected
Confusing join()'s index-based default with merge()'s column-based default
keyPoints: merge() matches on key columns (SQL-style join); join() defaults to matching on the index
concat() stacks DataFrames without matching any key
merge()'s default how='inner' silently drops unmatched rows from both sides
Comparing row counts and using indicator=True on a temporary outer merge catches silent drops

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes merge(), join(), and concat()
Correctly explains the inner-merge silent row-drop risk
Describes a concrete, practical way to catch the issue
Provides valid, relevant pandas code

questions.title: The Bias-Variance Tradeoff, in Plain Terms
questions.prompt: Explain the bias-variance tradeoff. What does it mean for a model to have high bias, what does it mean for a model to have high variance, and why can't you minimize both at the same time without limit?
questions.modelAnswer: Bias is error from a model being too simple to capture the real pattern in the data -- it makes systematically wrong assumptions, so it underfits, performing poorly on both training and new data in a consistent, predictable direction. Variance is error from a model being too sensitive to the specific training data it happened to see -- it overfits, picking up noise and quirks of that particular sample, so it performs very well on training data but swings unpredictably and performs worse on new data. The tradeoff exists because the two generally move in opposite directions as model complexity changes: a simpler model (like a shallow decision tree or a linear model with few features) tends to have higher bias but lower variance, while a more complex model (a deep tree, a model with many features and little regularization) tends to have lower bias but higher variance. You can't drive both to zero simultaneously with a fixed amount of data, because reducing bias generally means fitting the training data more closely, which is exactly what increases sensitivity to that specific sample. The practical goal is finding the sweet spot that minimizes total error -- bias squared plus variance plus irreducible noise -- not minimizing either term alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with the dartboard picture, because it's the clearest mental model. High bias is like consistently throwing darts that cluster together but far from the bullseye -- the model has a systematic, repeatable error in how it's wrong; a simple linear model trying to fit a clearly non-linear relationship is a classic example. High variance is like scattering darts all over the board, inconsistent from throw to throw -- the model's predictions swing a lot depending on exactly which training data it saw, which is what happens when a flexible model, like a very deep unregularized tree, starts memorizing noise specific to the training set. The reason you can't just minimize both forever is that the usual way to reduce bias is to let the model fit the training data more closely -- more features, more flexibility, less regularization -- and that's precisely the thing that makes it more sensitive to whatever particular sample it was trained on, which is variance. So in practice I'm not chasing zero bias or zero variance -- I'm looking at the total error on held-out data and tuning model complexity (via regularization strength, tree depth, number of features) to find wherever that total is lowest, which is almost never at either extreme.
commonMistakes: Describing high bias and high variance as the same thing, or using the terms interchangeably
Assuming a more complex model is always better because it reduces bias, ignoring the variance cost
Not connecting the tradeoff to a concrete lever (model complexity, regularization) that's actually adjustable
Thinking the goal is to eliminate bias or variance entirely rather than minimize their combined effect on held-out error
keyPoints: High bias = systematic underfitting error; high variance = overfitting, sample-sensitive error
Increasing model complexity typically lowers bias but raises variance, and vice versa
The two can't both be driven to zero with a fixed amount of data
The practical goal is minimizing total error on held-out data, not either term alone

questions.title: Why a Random Forest Usually Beats a Single Decision Tree
questions.prompt: A single decision tree and a random forest can be trained on the exact same data. Explain why the random forest usually generalizes better, specifically covering what bagging does and what the 'random' part of random forest adds beyond plain bagging.
questions.modelAnswer: A single decision tree, especially grown deep, tends to overfit -- it has low bias but high variance, since small changes in the training data can produce a very different tree. A random forest addresses the variance problem through bagging (bootstrap aggregating): it trains many trees, each on a different bootstrap sample (a random sample drawn with replacement from the training data), and then averages their predictions (for regression) or takes a majority vote (for classification). Averaging many high-variance, roughly-unbiased trees reduces variance substantially without increasing bias much, because the trees' individual errors tend to cancel out rather than compound. The 'random' part beyond plain bagging is feature randomness: at each split in each tree, random forest only considers a random subset of the available features, rather than every feature. This deliberately decorrelates the trees from each other -- without it, bagged trees built on similar bootstrap samples would often make very similar splits on the same dominant feature, which would limit how much averaging actually reduces variance. Less correlated trees average out more effectively, which is the real reason a random forest usually outperforms both a single tree and plain bagging of trees without feature randomness.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd break this into the two separate ideas, because people often blur them together. Bagging alone -- training many trees on different bootstrap samples and averaging their output -- already helps, because a single deep tree is a high-variance model: it can look wildly different if you perturb the training data even slightly, and averaging many such trees smooths that variance out, the same way averaging many noisy measurements gives you a steadier estimate than trusting just one. But random forest adds a second trick that plain bagging doesn't have: at every single split, it restricts each tree to a random subset of the features instead of letting it consider all of them. That sounds like it should make individual trees worse, and in isolation it does -- but it forces different trees to actually look at different signals and build somewhat different structure, instead of all converging on splitting on the one dominant feature in nearly the same way. Trees that are less correlated with each other benefit much more from averaging, because their individual mistakes are less likely to all point the same direction at once. So the real answer to 'why does random forest usually beat a single tree' is bagging reduces variance by averaging, and feature randomness makes that averaging actually effective by decorrelating the trees in the first place.
commonMistakes: Explaining only bagging and never mentioning the feature-subsampling part that gives random forest its name
Claiming random forest reduces bias, when its main benefit over a single tree is variance reduction
Not explaining why decorrelating the trees matters for how effective the averaging actually is
Assuming more trees always helps without bound, ignoring diminishing returns and added computation
keyPoints: A single deep tree has low bias but high variance
Bagging trains many trees on bootstrap samples and averages/votes, reducing variance
Feature randomness at each split decorrelates the trees beyond plain bagging
Less-correlated trees benefit more from averaging, which is why random forest typically outperforms plain bagging

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains bagging and why averaging reduces variance
Correctly explains the feature-randomness mechanism specifically
Explains why decorrelating trees improves the benefit of averaging
Correctly attributes the benefit to variance reduction, not bias reduction

questions.title: Logistic Regression: From Linear Score to Probability
questions.prompt: Explain how logistic regression turns a linear combination of features into a probability between 0 and 1. What role does the sigmoid function play, and what does a coefficient actually represent in terms of odds?
questions.modelAnswer: Logistic regression starts exactly like linear regression: it computes a linear combination of the features, z = b0 + b1*x1 + b2*x2 + ..., which can be any real number from negative to positive infinity. The problem is that a probability has to be between 0 and 1, so that raw linear score z can't be used directly as a probability. The sigmoid function, 1 / (1 + e^-z), solves this by squashing any real number into the (0, 1) range -- very negative z values map close to 0, very positive z values map close to 1, and z = 0 maps to exactly 0.5. Applying sigmoid to the linear score is what makes the output a valid probability. The coefficients themselves are most naturally interpreted in terms of log-odds, not probability directly: logistic regression is actually modeling the log-odds (log(p / (1-p))) as a linear function of the features, so a coefficient of b1 means that a one-unit increase in x1 increases the log-odds of the positive class by b1, holding other features constant. Exponentiating a coefficient (e^b1) converts that into an odds ratio -- how much the odds of the positive class multiply for a one-unit increase in that feature.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it in the order it actually happens mathematically. First, logistic regression computes the exact same thing linear regression would -- a weighted sum of the features, which can land anywhere on the real number line. That raw number by itself can't be a probability, since probabilities are stuck between 0 and 1. That's exactly the job of the sigmoid function: it takes that unbounded number and squeezes it into the 0-to-1 range, with large negative inputs squashed near 0, large positive inputs squashed near 1, and zero landing right at 0.5. So the full pipeline is: compute the linear score, then run it through sigmoid to get a probability. For the coefficients, I always clarify that they're not directly 'probability per unit of x' -- that would require accounting for the sigmoid's curve, which isn't constant. What's actually linear is the log-odds, log(p over 1 minus p), so a coefficient tells you how much the log-odds change per unit increase in that feature. If I exponentiate the coefficient, I get something more intuitive to explain to a stakeholder: an odds ratio, like 'a one-unit increase in this feature roughly doubles the odds of churn,' which is usually the version I'd actually say out loud rather than talking about log-odds directly.
questions.example:
z = b0 + b1*x1 + b2*x2
p = 1 / (1 + e^(-z))          # sigmoid converts z into a 0-1 probability

# Coefficient interpretation:
log(p / (1 - p)) = z          # the model is linear in log-odds, not in probability
odds_ratio = e^b1             # exponentiating converts a coefficient into an odds ratio
commonMistakes: Saying the coefficients represent a direct change in probability, ignoring the sigmoid's non-linearity
Forgetting that the linear part of the model is in log-odds space, not probability space
Describing the sigmoid as arbitrary rather than explaining why it's needed (bounding output to 0-1)
Confusing an odds ratio with a probability when communicating a coefficient to stakeholders
keyPoints: Logistic regression first computes an unbounded linear score from the features
The sigmoid function maps that score into a valid (0, 1) probability
The model is linear in log-odds, not in raw probability
Exponentiating a coefficient converts it into an interpretable odds ratio

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the linear score computed before sigmoid
Correctly explains the sigmoid function's role and shape
Correctly explains the log-odds interpretation of coefficients
Correctly describes converting a coefficient into an odds ratio

questions.title: Precision, Recall, and Why Accuracy Can Lie to You
questions.prompt: Define precision and recall for a binary classifier, explain the tradeoff between them, and explain why F1 score exists. Then explain a scenario where a model with 99% accuracy would actually be useless.
questions.modelAnswer: Precision is: of everything the model predicted as positive, what fraction actually was positive (TP / (TP + FP)) -- it answers 'when the model says yes, how often is it right?' Recall is: of everything that was actually positive, what fraction did the model catch (TP / (TP + FN)) -- it answers 'of all the real positives out there, how many did the model find?' There's a natural tradeoff because they respond oppositely to how aggressive the model's decision threshold is: lowering the threshold to flag more things as positive catches more real positives (raising recall) but also flags more false positives (lowering precision), and vice versa. F1 score exists because optimizing for one alone can be gamed trivially -- a model that predicts everything positive gets perfect recall but terrible precision, and a model that almost never predicts positive can get high precision but terrible recall. F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, which only scores well when both are reasonably good, punishing the case where one is near zero even if the other is near one. The 99% accuracy trap: if a dataset has 99% negative cases (like fraud detection, where fraud is rare), a model that simply predicts 'not fraud' for everything achieves 99% accuracy while catching zero actual fraud cases -- recall of 0% on the class that actually matters, making the model completely useless despite the impressive-sounding accuracy number.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd define both with the question they're actually answering, because that's more memorable than the formulas alone. Precision answers 'when my model raises its hand and says yes, how often is it actually right?' Recall answers 'of all the real positive cases that exist, how many did my model actually catch?' These pull against each other because of the threshold: if I make the model more trigger-happy about predicting positive, I'll catch more real positives (recall goes up) but I'll also catch more false alarms along the way (precision goes down), and tightening the threshold does the reverse. F1 exists because either one alone is too easy to game -- I could get perfect recall by just predicting positive for everything, which would be a terrible, useless model that also happens to have 100% recall. F1 is the harmonic mean specifically because it refuses to give a good score unless both numbers are decent; one near zero tanks the whole F1 score even if the other is perfect. The accuracy trap is the exact scenario I'd walk through in an interview: imagine a fraud dataset where only 1% of transactions are actually fraud. A model that just predicts 'not fraud' on every single transaction gets 99% accuracy and catches literally zero fraud -- the metric looks great and the model is worthless, which is exactly why I never trust accuracy alone on an imbalanced problem and always look at precision, recall, and the confusion matrix underneath it.
commonMistakes: Mixing up the denominators of precision and recall (FP vs. FN)
Describing F1 as a simple average of precision and recall instead of the harmonic mean, missing why it punishes imbalance between the two
Not connecting the precision/recall tradeoff to the decision threshold as the actual lever being adjusted
Trusting accuracy as a sufficient metric without checking class balance first
keyPoints: Precision = TP/(TP+FP); recall = TP/(TP+FN)
Lowering the classification threshold raises recall and lowers precision, and vice versa
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, punishing a large gap between them
High accuracy on an imbalanced dataset can hide zero recall on the class that matters

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines precision and recall
Correctly explains the threshold-driven tradeoff between them
Correctly explains F1's purpose as the harmonic mean
Gives a correct, concrete 99%-accuracy-but-useless scenario

questions.title: Top-2-per-group with a window function
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against AdventureWorks2012's Production.Product table that returns the two highest-priced products in each color, without using a correlated subquery.
questions.modelAnswer: The idiomatic way to solve 'top N per group' in T-SQL is PARTITION BY plus ROW_NUMBER(), wrapped in a CTE so the ranking column can be filtered afterward. PARTITION BY Color restarts the numbering at 1 for each color, and ORDER BY ListPrice DESC makes 1 the most expensive product in that color. You can't filter directly on ROW_NUMBER() in the same SELECT's WHERE clause because window functions are logically evaluated after WHERE -- that's why the CTE (or a subquery) is necessary.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the classic 'top N per group' problem, and the pattern I reach for every time is a CTE with ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by the grouping column. I avoid a correlated subquery with TOP 2 inside it because that approach re-executes once per outer row and doesn't scale well. Instead, I compute the rank once in a CTE, then just filter WHERE RankInColor <= 2 in the outer query. The one gotcha I always mention out loud in an interview: you cannot write WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) <= 2 directly in the same SELECT, because the WHERE clause is logically evaluated before window functions are computed -- that's exactly why the CTE wrapper is required, not just a style preference.
questions.example:
WITH Ranked AS (
    SELECT Name, Color, ListPrice,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Color ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS RankInColor
    FROM Production.Product
)
SELECT Name, Color, ListPrice
FROM Ranked
WHERE RankInColor <= 2
ORDER BY Color, RankInColor;
-- The CTE is required because ROW_NUMBER() can't be filtered in the same SELECT's WHERE clause.
commonMistakes: Trying to filter WHERE ROW_NUMBER() <= 2 directly in the same SELECT (not legal -- window functions evaluate after WHERE)
Forgetting PARTITION BY and ranking across the whole table instead of per color
Using TOP 2 with a correlated subquery per group, which is correct but far less efficient on large tables
Omitting ORDER BY inside OVER(), which leaves 'top' undefined
keyPoints: PARTITION BY restarts the ranking per group (per color here)
A CTE or subquery is required to filter on the window function's result
ORDER BY DESC inside OVER() makes rank 1 the highest price
This pattern generalizes to any 'top N per group' business question

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses ROW_NUMBER() with correct PARTITION BY and ORDER BY
Wraps it in a CTE/subquery to filter correctly
Query is syntactically valid and returns exactly 2 rows per color
Explains why filtering can't happen in the same SELECT's WHERE clause

questions.title: Temp table, table variable, or CTE?
questions.prompt: You need to hold an intermediate result set of about 500,000 rows, reuse it across three separate statements in a stored procedure, and would benefit from adding your own index to it. Which of #temp table, @table variable, or CTE would you choose, and why would the other two be worse choices here?
questions.modelAnswer: A #temp table is the right choice. It's a real, physically-stored table in tempdb, so SQL Server maintains real statistics on it (row counts), which lets the optimizer build a much smarter plan for a large result set, and you can explicitly add your own indexes to it. A table variable would be the wrong choice here: it also lives in tempdb, but historically has no maintained statistics, so on older compatibility levels the optimizer may assume just one row and badly under-allocate resources for 500,000 rows -- and while you can add inline PRIMARY KEY/UNIQUE constraints, you can't add arbitrary indexes the way you can on a #temp table. A CTE would also be the wrong choice: it isn't physically stored at all -- it's inlined into the query -- so referencing it in three separate statements could mean SQL Server re-runs its underlying query multiple times, and you can't add an index to something that was never materialized.
questions.professionalAnswer: Given the three constraints in the question -- large row count, reused across multiple statements, and wanting an index -- a #temp table wins on all three. The decision rule I use: CTEs are for one-time readability or recursion, not for reuse -- a CTE doesn't store anything, it's re-inlined at every reference, so touching it from three separate statements risks the underlying query running three separate times. Table variables are for small result sets inside a procedure where I want to avoid plan recompiles -- but historically they carry no real statistics, so the optimizer can badly misjudge a large one. A #temp table is the one option that's physically stored with real statistics the optimizer can use, and the only one of the three where I can explicitly add an index after the fact. For 500,000 rows reused three times, I'm reaching for #temp every time.
commonMistakes: Choosing a CTE for something reused across multiple statements, not realizing it may re-run its query each time
Choosing a table variable for a large result set, assuming it always performs the same as a temp table
Not mentioning that #temp tables maintain real statistics while table variables historically don't
Forgetting that CTEs can't be indexed at all, since nothing is actually materialized
keyPoints: #Temp tables are physically stored with maintained statistics and can be indexed
Table variables historically lack statistics, risking a poor plan on large sets
CTEs are inlined, not stored, and may re-execute their query on every reference
Choice depends on size, reuse, and whether an index is needed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly chooses the #temp table for this scenario
Correctly explains why a table variable would be worse here
Correctly explains why a CTE would be worse here

questions.title: Raising a custom business-rule error
questions.prompt: Write T-SQL that checks whether a discount percentage exceeds 50% and, if so, raises a custom error using the modern recommended syntax. Then show how you would log an error inside a CATCH block and still let it propagate to the caller.
questions.modelAnswer: THROW is the modern, recommended way to raise a custom error, taking an error number, a message, and a state, and raising it exactly as if SQL Server had generated it itself. For a business rule like a discount cap, you check the condition and THROW a custom error if it's violated. To log an error and still propagate it, use THROW with no arguments inside a CATCH block -- it re-raises the exact error that was just caught, unmodified, after whatever logging or cleanup logic runs first. RAISERROR is the older syntax, still common in existing code, with a different argument shape (message, severity, state) -- recognize it, but prefer THROW for new code.
questions.professionalAnswer: For the business rule check itself, I'd write a simple IF that tests the discount, and THROW a custom error number with a clear message if it's violated -- that's the modern, recommended way, and it's a one-liner. The more interesting half of this question is re-throwing from a CATCH block, because that's a pattern people often get wrong: they either swallow the error silently after logging it, or they try to reconstruct it with a new THROW statement and lose the original error details. The clean way is TRY/CATCH around the risky operation, log whatever you need to inside CATCH, and then just write THROW with no arguments -- that re-raises the exact error that was caught, unmodified, so the caller still sees the real failure instead of a sanitized stand-in.
questions.example:
-- Business rule check
IF @DiscountPercent > 50
    THROW 50000, 'Discount cannot exceed 50 percent.', 1;

-- Logging then re-throwing the original error
BEGIN TRY
    UPDATE Sales.SpecialOffer SET DiscountPct = @DiscountPercent WHERE SpecialOfferID = @ID;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    INSERT INTO ErrorLog (ErrorMessage, LoggedAt) VALUES (ERROR_MESSAGE(), GETDATE());
    THROW; -- re-raises the exact caught error, unmodified
END CATCH
commonMistakes: Using RAISERROR for new code instead of the modern, recommended THROW
Writing a new THROW statement inside CATCH instead of bare THROW, which loses the original error's details
Forgetting THROW's argument order is (error number, message, state) -- a different shape than RAISERROR's
Swallowing the error entirely after logging it, instead of re-throwing so the caller knows it failed
keyPoints: THROW is the modern, recommended way to raise a custom error
Bare THROW inside CATCH re-raises the exact original error
RAISERROR is the older syntax, still seen in legacy code
Logging an error doesn't have to mean swallowing it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses THROW to raise a custom business-rule error
Correctly uses TRY/CATCH with bare THROW to re-raise after logging

questions.title: Join Four Tables, Mixing INNER and LEFT
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against AdventureWorks2012 that returns each order line's product name, order date, and the customer's first and last name, including order lines for products that may no longer have a subcategory assigned. Use at least one LEFT JOIN alongside INNER JOINs.
questions.modelAnswer: This requires chaining four tables together: SalesOrderHeader (for the order date and customer link), SalesOrderDetail (the order lines), Product (for the product name), and Person (for the customer's name), while also reaching ProductSubcategory with a LEFT JOIN so that products missing a subcategory still appear instead of being silently excluded. Each JOIN connects to whatever table already has the needed column available, not necessarily the very first table named in FROM — for instance, the join to Product uses ProductID from SalesOrderDetail, introduced by the join just before it. The LEFT JOIN to ProductSubcategory is the one deliberate choice: an INNER JOIN there would drop any order line whose product has a NULL ProductSubcategoryID, which is exactly the scenario the question asks to preserve.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this one join at a time rather than writing the whole thing at once, because that's the only way to keep four tables straight. I start from SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail joined on SalesOrderID, since that's the backbone of the query. Then I bring in Product on ProductID to get the product name, and Person on CustomerID (really BusinessEntityID) to get the name. All three of those are INNER JOINs because I genuinely need a match on all of them for the row to make sense. The one place I'd stop and think is ProductSubcategory — the question specifically says some products might not have one, and an INNER JOIN there would quietly drop those order lines from the result with no warning. That's exactly the signal to use LEFT JOIN instead, so a product with a NULL ProductSubcategoryID still shows up, just with NULL in the subcategory column rather than vanishing from the report entirely.
questions.example:
SELECT soh.OrderDate, p.Name AS ProductName, per.FirstName, per.LastName, ps.Name AS SubcategoryName
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader AS soh
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON soh.SalesOrderID = sod.SalesOrderID
INNER JOIN Production.Product AS p
    ON sod.ProductID = p.ProductID
INNER JOIN Person.Person AS per
    ON soh.CustomerID = per.BusinessEntityID
LEFT JOIN Production.ProductSubcategory AS ps
    ON p.ProductSubcategoryID = ps.ProductSubcategoryID;
commonMistakes: Using INNER JOIN on ProductSubcategory, which silently drops any order line for a product missing a subcategory
Joining to the wrong table's column (e.g. trying to reach ProductID directly from SalesOrderHeader, which doesn't have it)
Forgetting table aliases on a four-table query, making it unreadable and error-prone to debug
Not noticing that CustomerID on SalesOrderHeader maps to BusinessEntityID on Person.Person, not a column literally named CustomerID there
keyPoints: Each JOIN can reference any table already available earlier in the query, not just the first one
LEFT JOIN preserves rows that would otherwise be dropped by a stricter INNER JOIN
Mixing INNER and LEFT JOIN in one query is normal when different relationships have different guarantees
Clear aliases are essential once a query joins more than two or three tables

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly joins all four required tables
Uses LEFT JOIN specifically for ProductSubcategory
Query is syntactically valid and returns the correct columns
Explains why LEFT JOIN was chosen there instead of INNER JOIN

questions.title: Left-Merging Orders to Customers and Handling the Resulting NaNs
questions.prompt: You have an orders DataFrame and a customers DataFrame, both with a customer_id column. Write pandas code to left-merge orders onto customers so every order is kept even if its customer record is missing, then explain how you'd handle the NaN values that merge introduces in the customer columns for unmatched orders.
questions.modelAnswer: A left merge (how='left') keeps every row from orders regardless of whether its customer_id finds a match in customers, which is exactly what's needed here since the goal is to never lose an order. For any order whose customer_id has no match, pandas fills every column that came from customers with NaN. How to handle those NaNs depends on what the column means and what the data will be used for: for a categorical field like customer_segment, filling with an explicit placeholder like 'Unknown' is usually better than leaving NaN, so downstream grouping and filtering don't silently drop those rows. For a numeric field, filling with 0 can be actively wrong if 0 is a valid value elsewhere -- it's often more honest to leave it NaN (so aggregate functions correctly exclude it) or to flag it with a separate boolean column like has_customer_record, so anyone using the data later can explicitly decide how to treat the unmatched orders rather than silently inheriting a filled value's meaning.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this as a straightforward left merge first, then think carefully about the NaNs rather than rushing to fill them. merged = orders.merge(customers, on='customer_id', how='left') keeps every single order row, and any order whose customer_id doesn't exist in customers just gets NaN in all the customer-side columns. The part I actually spend time on is deciding what those NaNs should become, because 'just fillna(0)' is a common shortcut that can be genuinely wrong -- if a numeric column like customer_lifetime_value gets filled with 0, that's not 'we don't know this value,' it's 'this customer has spent exactly zero,' which is a different and false claim. My usual approach is to add an explicit has_customer_record boolean column first, so the information 'this merge didn't find a match' is preserved and visible, and then decide fill values column by column based on what each one actually means -- a categorical gets an explicit 'Unknown' label, while I'd usually leave numeric fields as NaN so later aggregations (mean, sum) handle them correctly rather than quietly treating a missing customer as a zero-value customer.
questions.example:
merged = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left")

# Preserve the fact that a match was missing, before any filling
merged["has_customer_record"] = merged["customer_id"].isin(customers["customer_id"])

# Fill categorical placeholders explicitly
merged["customer_segment"] = merged["customer_segment"].fillna("Unknown")

# Leave numeric fields as NaN rather than a misleading 0
# merged["lifetime_value"] stays NaN; aggregations will correctly exclude it
commonMistakes: Using how='inner' by habit, silently dropping orders with no matching customer record
Filling numeric NaNs with 0 without considering whether 0 is a valid, different value in that column
Not tracking which rows actually had a missing match before filling, losing that information
Forgetting to specify the join key explicitly with on=, risking an unintended merge on overlapping column names
keyPoints: how='left' preserves every row from orders regardless of a customer match
Unmatched rows get NaN in every column sourced from the right-side DataFrame
A numeric fillna(0) can be factually wrong, not just a style choice
Tracking which rows were unmatched (before filling) preserves information for downstream use

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correct left merge on the right key
Correctly explains why NaNs appear for unmatched rows
Gives a thoughtful, column-type-aware approach to handling the NaNs
Notes the risk of a careless fillna(0) on numeric columns

questions.title: Parsing a Messy Date Column and a Numeric-Looking String Column
questions.prompt: A raw CSV loads a signup_date column as plain strings in inconsistent formats (some 'MM/DD/YYYY', some 'YYYY-MM-DD'), and a price column as strings with dollar signs and commas, like '$1,200.00'. Write pandas code to clean both columns into proper dtypes, and explain what you'd check afterward to confirm the conversion worked correctly.
questions.modelAnswer: For the date column, pd.to_datetime() can often infer mixed formats automatically, but when formats are genuinely inconsistent it's safer to pass errors='coerce' so unparseable values become NaT (a missing-datetime marker) instead of raising and stopping the whole pipeline. For the price column, the dollar sign and comma have to be stripped from the string before it can be converted to a float -- str.replace() for both characters, followed by astype(float) or pd.to_numeric(errors='coerce'). After conversion, I'd check for NaN/NaT counts introduced by the conversion (df['signup_date'].isna().sum() before and after, same for price) to see how many rows failed to parse, and I'd spot-check a sample of the original string values that produced NaT/NaN to understand whether there's a format pattern I'm missing rather than just data that's genuinely bad.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd handle these one at a time because they fail in different ways. For the date column, my first move is pd.to_datetime(df['signup_date'], errors='coerce') -- pandas is often smart enough to infer a mix of formats, but errors='coerce' is the safety net: instead of the whole operation blowing up on one malformed string, that specific row becomes NaT and everything else still converts. For the price column, the string has characters a float conversion can't handle at all, so I strip them first -- df['price'].str.replace('$', '', regex=False).str.replace(',', '', regex=False) -- and then convert with pd.to_numeric(errors='coerce') for the same safety-net reason. The step I never skip afterward is checking how many NaN or NaT values got introduced that weren't there as nulls originally -- df['price'].isna().sum() before versus after tells me exactly how many rows failed to parse. If that number is non-trivial, I go look at the actual original string values behind those failures, because it usually means there's a format I didn't anticipate (a different currency symbol, a date with a two-digit year) rather than the data genuinely being garbage.
questions.example:
df["signup_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["signup_date"], errors="coerce")

df["price"] = (
    df["price"]
    .str.replace("$", "", regex=False)
    .str.replace(",", "", regex=False)
)
df["price"] = pd.to_numeric(df["price"], errors="coerce")

# Verification
print(df["signup_date"].isna().sum(), df["price"].isna().sum())
bad_rows = df[df["price"].isna()]
print(bad_rows)  # inspect the original strings behind the failed conversions
commonMistakes: Calling astype(float) directly on a string with '$' and ',' still in it, which raises an error
