questions.title: Detecting Outliers With the IQR Method
questions.prompt: Write Python code using the IQR (interquartile range) method to flag outliers in a numeric column, and explain why you'd want to look at a histogram or box plot of the column before deciding to remove anything the method flags.
questions.modelAnswer: The IQR method computes Q1 (25th percentile) and Q3 (75th percentile) of a column, finds the interquartile range IQR = Q3 - Q1, and flags any value below Q1 - 1.5*IQR or above Q3 + 1.5*IQR as an outlier -- the 1.5 multiplier is a conventional default, not a universal law. Before removing anything flagged this way, I'd look at a histogram or box plot first, because the IQR rule is a purely statistical definition that doesn't know anything about the business context: a flagged value might be a genuine data error (a negative age, a price with an extra zero typed in), or it might be a real, legitimate extreme value (a genuinely large enterprise order in a mostly-small-business dataset) that a model should actually learn from, not discard. Visualizing the distribution also reveals whether the column is skewed to begin with, in which case the IQR method -- which assumes a roughly symmetric distribution -- may flag a large fraction of real, valid values on the heavier tail as 'outliers' when they're just an expected part of a skewed distribution.
questions.professionalAnswer: The code itself is simple -- compute Q1 and Q3 with quantile(), get the IQR, and flag anything outside Q1 minus 1.5 times IQR to Q3 plus 1.5 times IQR. The 1.5 multiplier is just a convention, not a rule carved in stone, so I treat the flag as 'worth looking at,' not 'automatically wrong.' That's exactly why I always pull up a histogram or box plot of the column before deciding what to do with anything flagged. The IQR formula has no idea whether a flagged value is a data-entry mistake -- someone fairly plausibly typed an extra zero into a price field -- or a real, important data point, like one enterprise customer placing a genuinely huge order in a dataset mostly full of small retail purchases. Those two situations call for completely different responses: one is a bug to fix or drop, the other is real signal a model should probably see. Visualizing the distribution also tells me whether the column is naturally skewed, because the 1.5xIQR rule was built assuming something close to a normal-ish shape -- on a heavily right-skewed column like income or order size, it can flag a large chunk of the legitimate upper tail as 'outliers' when that's just how the real data looks.
questions.example:
q1 = df["order_total"].quantile(0.25)
q3 = df["order_total"].quantile(0.75)
iqr = q3 - q1
lower = q1 - 1.5 * iqr
upper = q3 + 1.5 * iqr

outliers = df[(df["order_total"] < lower) | (df["order_total"] > upper)]
print(len(outliers), "flagged rows out of", len(df))

# Always visualize before deciding what to do with them:
# df["order_total"].plot(kind="box")
# df["order_total"].plot(kind="hist", bins=50)
commonMistakes: Automatically dropping every row the IQR rule flags without inspecting what they actually are
Treating the 1.5 multiplier as a fixed rule rather than an adjustable convention
Applying the IQR method to a clearly skewed distribution without recognizing it will over-flag the real tail
Not distinguishing a data-entry error from a legitimate extreme value before deciding to drop or keep a flagged row
keyPoints: IQR outlier bounds are Q1 - 1.5*IQR and Q3 + 1.5*IQR, with 1.5 as a common convention
A flagged value is a candidate to investigate, not automatically an error to remove
Visualizing the distribution first reveals whether a flagged point is a mistake or real signal
Skewed distributions can cause the rule to over-flag a legitimate heavy tail

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements the IQR bounds and flags outliers
Explains why visualization should precede any removal decision
Distinguishes a data error from a legitimate extreme value
Notes the method's assumption of a roughly symmetric distribution

questions.title: Running and Interpreting a Two-Sample t-Test
questions.prompt: You want to know whether average session duration differs between users on a new website layout versus the old one. Write Python code (using scipy) to run an independent two-sample t-test, and explain how you'd interpret the resulting p-value at a 0.05 significance level.
questions.modelAnswer: scipy.stats.ttest_ind() runs an independent (unpaired) two-sample t-test, comparing the means of two independent groups -- here, session durations for the new-layout group versus the old-layout group. It returns a t-statistic and a p-value. Before trusting the result, it's worth checking the test's assumptions loosely hold: the two groups should be independent (which they are, different users), and the test assumes the data is reasonably close to normally distributed, or that sample sizes are large enough for the central limit theorem to make that less critical. To interpret the p-value at alpha = 0.05: if p < 0.05, there's enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis that the two groups have equal mean session duration, so I'd conclude there's a statistically significant difference. If p >= 0.05, I don't have enough evidence to reject the null -- which is not the same as proving the means are equal, just that this sample didn't provide strong enough evidence of a difference. Either way, I'd also look at the actual size of the difference (the effect size), not just whether it's 'significant,' since a statistically significant difference of 2 seconds might not matter to the business at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: The code is short -- scipy.stats.ttest_ind(new_layout_durations, old_layout_durations) -- but the interpretation is where I'd spend the actual conversation. Before even looking at the p-value, I'd sanity-check the setup: are these genuinely independent samples (different users, not the same users measured twice, which would need a paired test instead), and is the sample size reasonable so the test's normality assumption isn't a serious concern. Once I have the p-value, my interpretation at alpha=0.05 is straightforward but I phrase it carefully: if p is below 0.05, that's enough evidence to say the difference in average session duration is unlikely to be due to chance alone, so I'd call it statistically significant. If p is above 0.05, I explicitly do not say 'the layouts have no effect' -- I say we don't have strong enough evidence in this sample to detect a difference, which leaves room for either a true null effect or a real effect we didn't have enough data to detect. And regardless of which side of 0.05 it lands on, I always pull the actual mean difference in seconds alongside the p-value, because a tiny, genuinely real difference can still be statistically significant with enough data and still be completely irrelevant to any business decision.
questions.example:
from scipy import stats

t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_ind(new_layout_durations, old_layout_durations)
print(f"t = {t_stat:.3f}, p = {p_value:.4f}")

if p_value < 0.05:
    print("Statistically significant difference at alpha=0.05")
else:
    print("Not enough evidence of a difference at alpha=0.05")
commonMistakes: Using a paired t-test (ttest_rel) when the samples are actually independent users, or vice versa
Saying a p-value above 0.05 'proves' there's no difference, rather than just insufficient evidence
Reporting only the p-value without also reporting the actual effect size (the mean difference)
Not checking that the two groups being compared are genuinely independent before choosing the test
keyPoints: scipy.stats.ttest_ind() compares the means of two independent samples
p < 0.05 at alpha=0.05 is enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis of equal means
p >= 0.05 means insufficient evidence of a difference, not proof the means are equal
Effect size (the actual mean difference) should be reported alongside the p-value

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses scipy's independent two-sample t-test
Correctly interprets p < 0.05 and p >= 0.05 without overstating either
Checks or mentions the test's independence/normality assumptions
Notes the importance of effect size alongside significance

questions.title: Engineering New Features From Raw Timestamp and Category Columns
questions.prompt: Given a transactions DataFrame with a raw timestamp column and a merchant_category string column, write pandas code to engineer at least three new features that would plausibly help a fraud-detection model, and explain why each one might carry predictive signal.
questions.modelAnswer: From the timestamp, I'd extract hour_of_day and day_of_week -- fraud often clusters at unusual hours (like 3am) or follows different patterns on weekends versus weekdays, and a raw timestamp itself is far too high-cardinality for a model to learn useful structure from directly. I'd also engineer is_weekend as a simple boolean, since weekend spending patterns can differ meaningfully from weekday ones. From merchant_category, rather than leaving it as a high-cardinality raw string, I'd compute a feature like merchant_category_fraud_rate -- a historical fraud rate per category computed from training data only, which gives the model a direct numeric signal about how risky that category has historically been, without needing it to memorize dozens of one-hot encoded categories. Each of these converts a raw, hard-to-use column into a feature a model can actually extract a pattern from -- the point of feature engineering here isn't making up arbitrary numbers, it's encoding domain knowledge (fraud timing patterns, category risk) into a form the model's algorithm can use.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start from what's actually predictive about fraud, not just mechanically transform columns. Time matters a lot for fraud -- a transaction at 3am is more suspicious on average than one at 2pm, so I'd pull hour_of_day out of the raw timestamp. Day-of-week patterns matter too, so day_of_week and a simple is_weekend flag give the model that signal without forcing it to parse a raw datetime, which most models can't use directly anyway. For merchant_category, my instinct is to avoid just one-hot encoding fifty categories and instead compute something with more direct signal: a historical fraud rate per category, calculated only from the training data to avoid leaking future information into past rows. That single numeric feature often carries more useful signal for a model than a long list of category dummy variables, because it directly encodes 'how risky has this category actually been historically' instead of asking the model to learn that relationship on its own from sparse one-hot columns. The theme across all three: I'm not inventing arbitrary features, I'm translating something I already know matters for fraud -- timing, category risk -- into a numeric form the model's algorithm can actually use.
questions.example:
df["hour_of_day"] = df["timestamp"].dt.hour
df["day_of_week"] = df["timestamp"].dt.dayofweek
df["is_weekend"] = df["day_of_week"].isin([5, 6])

# Category risk feature computed from TRAINING data only, to avoid leakage
category_fraud_rate = train_df.groupby("merchant_category")["is_fraud"].mean()
df["merchant_category_fraud_rate"] = df["merchant_category"].map(category_fraud_rate)

Computing the category fraud rate using the full dataset instead of training data only, leaking label information
Engineering features with no articulated reason they'd be predictive, rather than ones grounded in domain knowledge
keyPoints: Raw timestamps should be decomposed into usable components (hour, day of week, weekend flag)
A historical-rate feature can be more useful than high-cardinality one-hot encoding
Any rate/target-derived feature must be computed from training data only to avoid leakage
Good feature engineering encodes domain knowledge, not arbitrary transformations

questions.title: Running k-Means and Choosing k With the Elbow Method
questions.prompt: Write Python/scikit-learn code to run k-means clustering on a numeric customer dataset for several candidate values of k, and explain how you'd use the elbow method to pick a reasonable k. What's a limitation of the elbow method you'd mention?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd fit KMeans for a range of k values (say 2 through 10), recording each model's inertia -- the sum of squared distances from each point to its assigned cluster centroid -- and plot k against inertia. Inertia always decreases as k increases (more clusters can always fit the data at least as well), so the goal isn't to find where inertia is lowest, which would trivially be the largest k tried. Instead, the elbow method looks for the point where the rate of decrease sharply flattens -- the 'elbow' in the curve -- reasoning that adding clusters beyond that point gives rapidly diminishing improvement for the added complexity. A real limitation: the elbow point is often genuinely ambiguous -- many real datasets produce a smooth curve with no obvious bend, making the choice of k subjective and dependent on who's looking at the plot. For that reason, I'd usually pair the elbow method with another check, like the silhouette score, which measures how well-separated the clusters actually are, rather than relying on inertia's elbow alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mechanics are simple: loop over a range of k values, fit KMeans for each, and record model.inertia_, then plot k on the x-axis against inertia on the y-axis. The shape I'm looking for is the elbow -- inertia drops fast at first as you add clusters, then the drop flattens out, and the k where that flattening happens is the candidate choice, because beyond that point you're adding model complexity for very little actual improvement in how tightly points cluster around their centroid. I always mention the real limitation out loud though: on a lot of real datasets, that curve is smooth with no sharp bend at all, and 'where does this flatten' ends up being a judgment call that two people could reasonably disagree on just by eyeballing the same plot. Because of that, I don't treat the elbow method as the final word -- I'd usually also compute the silhouette score for the same range of k values, which actually measures how distinct and well-separated the resulting clusters are rather than just how low the inertia got, and use the two together rather than trusting the elbow plot in isolation.
questions.example:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

inertias = []
for k in range(2, 11):
    model = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42, n_init=10)
    model.fit(X_scaled)
    inertias.append(model.inertia_)

# Plot k vs inertia, look for the elbow
# plt.plot(range(2, 11), inertias, marker="o")

from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
sil_scores = []
for k in range(2, 11):
    labels = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42, n_init=10).fit_predict(X_scaled)
    sil_scores.append(silhouette_score(X_scaled, labels))
commonMistakes: Choosing the k with the lowest inertia overall, missing that inertia always decreases as k grows
Not scaling the numeric features before k-means, which is distance-based and sensitive to feature scale
Treating the elbow point as objective when it's often genuinely ambiguous on real data
Relying on the elbow method alone without a second check like silhouette score
keyPoints: Inertia is the sum of squared distances to assigned centroids, and always decreases as k increases
The elbow method looks for where the inertia-vs-k curve flattens, not where inertia is lowest
Features should be scaled before k-means since it's distance-based
The elbow is often ambiguous in practice; silhouette score is a useful complementary check

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly fits k-means across a range of k and records inertia
Correctly explains the elbow method's logic
Mentions feature scaling as a prerequisite for k-means
Correctly identifies the ambiguity limitation and a complementary check

questions.title: Building a scikit-learn Pipeline With ColumnTransformer
questions.prompt: You have a dataset with a mix of numeric columns (needing scaling) and categorical columns (needing one-hot encoding), followed by a logistic regression classifier. Write scikit-learn code using ColumnTransformer and Pipeline to handle this correctly, and explain the main benefit of wrapping everything in a Pipeline rather than preprocessing manually before calling fit().
questions.modelAnswer: ColumnTransformer lets you apply different preprocessing to different columns in one object: a StandardScaler on the numeric columns and a OneHotEncoder on the categorical columns, combined into a single transformer. Wrapping that ColumnTransformer together with the final classifier (LogisticRegression) inside a Pipeline chains them into one object that implements fit(), predict(), and score() as a single unit. The main benefit over manual preprocessing is leakage prevention combined with convenience: when you call cross_val_score or GridSearchCV on a Pipeline, the preprocessing steps (like the scaler's mean/std or the encoder's categories) are refit from scratch on only each training fold, not on the full dataset beforehand -- which is exactly correct behavior, since fitting the scaler on the full dataset before splitting would let information from the validation/test fold leak into training. Manually scaling the whole dataset once before doing cross-validation is a subtle but real leakage bug that a Pipeline avoids automatically, and it also means the exact same fitted preprocessing steps are guaranteed to be reused consistently at prediction time on new data.
questions.professionalAnswer: The structure is: build a ColumnTransformer that routes the numeric columns through a StandardScaler and the categorical columns through a OneHotEncoder, specifying which column names go to which transformer. Then I wrap that ColumnTransformer and the LogisticRegression model together inside a single Pipeline, so the whole thing -- preprocessing and model -- behaves as one estimator with one fit() call. The reason I always reach for this instead of manually scaling and encoding the DataFrame once up front is leakage, and it's a real bug I've seen people ship without realizing it: if you fit a StandardScaler on the entire dataset before doing cross-validation or a train/test split, the scaler's mean and standard deviation have already 'seen' the test data, so your evaluation is subtly optimistic in a way that won't hold up in production. Put the preprocessing inside the Pipeline instead, and every time cross-validation refits a fold, the scaler and encoder refit from scratch on only that fold's training data -- no leakage, and I also get the convenience of calling fit/predict on one object instead of manually replaying the same preprocessing steps every time I want to score new data.
questions.example:
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

numeric_cols = ["age", "income"]
categorical_cols = ["region", "plan_type"]

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", StandardScaler(), numeric_cols),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical_cols),
])

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("preprocess", preprocessor),
    ("model", LogisticRegression()),
])

pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
pipe.score(X_test, y_test)
commonMistakes: Scaling and encoding the full dataset once before splitting or cross-validating, leaking information
Forgetting handle_unknown='ignore' on the encoder, which crashes on an unseen category at prediction time
Applying the same transformer to all columns instead of routing numeric and categorical separately
Not realizing a Pipeline's main value during cross-validation is refitting preprocessing per fold
keyPoints: ColumnTransformer routes different preprocessing to different column subsets
A Pipeline chains preprocessing and the model into a single fit/predict unit
The key benefit is leakage prevention: preprocessing refits per fold during cross-validation
A Pipeline also guarantees consistent preprocessing is reapplied at prediction time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly builds a ColumnTransformer with appropriate transformers per column type
Correctly wraps the preprocessor and model in a Pipeline
Correctly explains the leakage-prevention benefit during cross-validation

questions.title: k-Fold Cross-Validation: Running It and Reporting the Result Honestly
questions.prompt: Write scikit-learn code to perform 5-fold cross-validation on a model and report the mean and standard deviation of the scores. Why is reporting both numbers more honest than reporting just the mean?
questions.modelAnswer: cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5) splits the data into 5 folds, trains on 4 and evaluates on the 1 held out, rotating which fold is held out each time, and returns an array of 5 scores. Reporting the mean gives a single, more stable estimate of expected performance than any one train/test split alone, since a single split's score depends partly on luck in exactly how that one split happened to fall. But the standard deviation across the 5 scores matters just as much: if the scores are something like [0.81, 0.79, 0.82, 0.80, 0.78], a mean of 0.80 is a trustworthy, stable estimate. If the scores are instead [0.95, 0.60, 0.85, 0.75, 0.85], the same mean of 0.80 is hiding real instability -- the model's performance swings wildly depending on which data it happens to see, which is important information a single mean number completely erases. Reporting the mean alone can make a genuinely unreliable model look just as trustworthy as a genuinely stable one with the identical average score.
questions.professionalAnswer: The code is one line -- scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5) -- but the number I actually care about reporting is two numbers, not one: scores.mean() and scores.std(). The reason is that a mean by itself can be deeply misleading about how much to trust the model. Two different models could both report a mean accuracy of 0.80 -- one with scores clustered tightly around 0.80 across all five folds, and another that swings from 0.60 on one fold to 0.95 on another, averaging out to the same 0.80 purely by coincidence. Those are not equally trustworthy models, and a mean-only report treats them as identical. The standard deviation is what actually surfaces that difference -- a small standard deviation says the model performs consistently regardless of which slice of data it saw, while a large standard deviation is a warning sign that performance is highly sensitive to the specific data split, which usually means I should dig into why, maybe an insufficient sample size, a feature that's unstable, or a stray outlier fold. I treat 'mean plus spread' as the minimum honest way to report any cross-validation result.
questions.example:
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5, scoring="accuracy")
print(f"Mean: {scores.mean():.3f}, Std: {scores.std():.3f}")
print("Individual fold scores:", scores)
commonMistakes: Reporting only the mean cross-validation score without the standard deviation
Not recognizing that two models with the same mean score can have very different reliability
Treating a high standard deviation as unimportant rather than a signal worth investigating
Using too few folds on a small dataset, producing noisy per-fold scores that are hard to interpret
keyPoints: cross_val_score returns one score per fold, not a single number
The mean estimates expected performance more stably than any single split
The standard deviation reveals how consistent that performance actually is across folds
Two models with identical means can have very different reliability if their spreads differ

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly runs 5-fold cross-validation
Correctly computes and reports both mean and standard deviation
Explains clearly why the standard deviation matters alongside the mean
Code is valid, runnable scikit-learn

questions.title: Diagnosing a deadlock between two ETL jobs
questions.prompt: Two nightly stored procedures occasionally fail with a deadlock error when they run at overlapping times, each updating the same two tables. Explain what a deadlock is, how SQL Server resolves it automatically, and two concrete things you'd change to prevent it from recurring.
questions.modelAnswer: Blocking happens whenever one transaction needs a lock another transaction already holds, and simply waits -- this is normal and expected. A deadlock is the special case where Transaction A is waiting on a lock held by Transaction B, while B is simultaneously waiting on a lock held by A -- neither can ever proceed. SQL Server detects this automatically and picks one transaction as the 'deadlock victim,' rolling it back and raising an error, while the other transaction proceeds normally. To prevent recurrence: (1) access the two tables in the same order in both procedures -- a common deadlock cause is two transactions locking the same two tables in opposite order; and (2) keep transactions as short as possible, doing only what genuinely needs to be atomic inside BEGIN/COMMIT, so locks are held for the shortest possible window and the overlap that triggers the deadlock has a smaller chance of occurring.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by reassuring whoever's asking that blocking itself isn't a bug -- it's how isolation is enforced any time two transactions genuinely need the same data at the same moment. A deadlock is the specific, more serious case: A is waiting on a lock B holds, B is waiting on a lock A holds, and neither can ever win -- it's a true standoff. SQL Server doesn't just hang forever; it detects the cycle and picks a 'deadlock victim' to roll back automatically, which is why the application sees an error and needs to retry. For the actual fix, the first thing I'd check is whether both procedures touch the two tables in a different order -- that's the single most common cause, and standardizing the access order so both procedures always touch, say, Table A before Table B usually eliminates it outright. Second, I'd look at whether either transaction is doing more than it needs to inside BEGIN/COMMIT -- unrelated reads, validation logic -- and trim the transaction down to just the atomic part, since shorter transactions hold locks for less time and collide less often.
commonMistakes: Treating a deadlock the same as ordinary blocking -- blocking is normal, a deadlock is a genuine, unresolvable standoff
Assuming SQL Server will just hang forever instead of recognizing it auto-detects and resolves deadlocks
Fixing the symptom by adding a retry loop in the application without addressing the inconsistent table access order
Making a transaction longer by adding error handling or logging inside it, which increases lock duration
keyPoints: Blocking is normal; a deadlock is two transactions waiting on each other with no way out
SQL Server auto-detects deadlocks and rolls back a chosen 'victim' transaction
The victim's application should retry the transaction
Accessing tables in a consistent order across procedures prevents most deadlocks
Shortening transactions reduces how long locks are held and how often collisions occur

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes blocking from a deadlock
Correctly explains SQL Server's automatic deadlock resolution
Proposes consistent table access order as a concrete fix
Proposes shortening transactions as a concrete fix

questions.title: A query got slow after it used to be fast
questions.prompt: A report query that filters WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2013 used to run instantly and now takes minutes as the table has grown. There is an index on OrderDate. Diagnose why the index isn't helping, and rewrite the WHERE clause so it is.
questions.modelAnswer: The predicate is non-SARGable: wrapping the OrderDate column in the YEAR() function forces SQL Server to compute YEAR(OrderDate) for every single row before it can compare against 2013, which means the index on the raw OrderDate column can't be used -- it stores actual dates, not year-extracted values. This was barely noticeable on a small table (a full scan of a few hundred rows is instant either way), but as the table grows into the millions of rows, the same non-SARGable predicate turns a sub-second query into one that takes minutes. The fix is to rewrite the condition so the column itself is left untouched, and transform the comparison value instead: WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2014-01-01'. This asks the identical logical question but lets SQL Server use the index on OrderDate to jump directly to the matching range.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a textbook SARGability problem, and the giveaway is right there in the WHERE clause -- there's a function wrapped around the column. Any time I see YEAR(SomeDateColumn), UPPER(SomeColumn), or similar, my first instinct is: the index on that raw column can't be used, because SQL Server would have to transform every row's value before it could compare it, and an index doesn't store transformed values. The reason it 'used to be fast' is simply table size -- a full scan is invisible on a small table and brutal on a large one, so this kind of bug often doesn't show up until data volume grows past some threshold. The fix is always the same shape: stop transforming the column, and transform the comparison value instead. Instead of asking 'what year is this date in,' I ask 'is this date within the 2013 calendar year range' -- same answer, but now the raw OrderDate column is untouched in the comparison, so the existing index can be used for a range scan instead of a full scan.
commonMistakes: Blaming the index itself ('the index must be corrupt/fragmented') instead of the predicate wrapping the column
Rewriting to BETWEEN '2013-01-01' AND '2013-12-31' and accidentally excluding rows with a time component on Dec 31
Not recognizing other common non-SARGable patterns like UPPER(column) = 'X' or a leading-wildcard LIKE '%text'
Assuming the problem only appears with YEAR() and missing that any function on the column causes the same issue
keyPoints: SARGable means the predicate can use an index directly; non-SARGable forces a full scan
Wrapping the column in a function (YEAR, UPPER, etc.) makes a predicate non-SARGable
Fix by transforming the comparison value instead of the column
The performance gap only becomes visible as table size grows

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the predicate as non-SARGable and explains why
Correctly explains why this matters more as the table grows
Provides a correct, equivalent SARGable rewrite

questions.title: A report is hanging, but there's no deadlock error
questions.prompt: Users report that a dashboard query has been 'just spinning' for several minutes, but no deadlock error ever appears. Explain the difference between this situation and a deadlock, how you'd identify the actual head blocker, and what you'd check before deciding to kill the blocking session.
questions.modelAnswer: This is ordinary blocking, not a deadlock -- a deadlock is a genuine standoff that SQL Server detects and resolves automatically within seconds by killing a victim; it never just hangs indefinitely. Plain blocking, by contrast, can hang as long as whatever is holding the lock keeps holding it, because there's no cycle for SQL Server to detect -- one session is simply waiting its turn behind another, and nothing resolves that automatically. To find the actual head blocker, I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests, specifically looking at the blocking_session_id column -- the session with a non-zero blocking_session_id is being blocked, and the session that ID points to (which itself usually shows blocking_session_id = 0) is the head blocker actually holding the lock everyone's waiting on. Before killing that session, I'd check what it's actually doing -- its SQL text, and whether it's an open, uncommitted transaction (an application that opened a transaction and is sitting idle, or a long-running batch job that's legitimately mid-write). Killing a session mid-write rolls back whatever it was doing, which can be worse than the wait itself if it's a large, mostly-finished operation -- so I'd rather understand what it's doing and consider letting it finish or committing/rolling it back cleanly than reflexively kill it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd clarify, because it changes the whole response, is that this isn't a deadlock -- SQL Server resolves deadlocks on its own, usually within seconds, by picking a victim and rolling it back. If nothing has errored and the query is just sitting there, that's plain blocking: one session waiting on a lock another session is holding, with no cycle, so nothing forces a resolution automatically. My first query is always against sys.dm_exec_requests, looking at blocking_session_id -- that tells me directly who's blocked and, by following the chain, who the actual head blocker is, as opposed to the session that looks blocked but is itself only blocked by someone else further up. Once I've got the head blocker's session ID, I'd pull its actual SQL text and check whether it's sitting inside an open transaction that was never committed, versus genuinely mid-execution on a big write. That distinction decides what I do next -- if it's an application bug that opened a transaction and forgot to close it, killing the session is reasonable and I'd also flag that bug separately. If it's a legitimate long-running batch load that's 90% done, killing it rolls back all of that work and probably makes things worse, so I'd rather let it finish, or coordinate with whoever owns that job before touching it.
questions.example:
-- Find who's blocking whom
SELECT session_id, blocking_session_id, wait_type, wait_time, status
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests
WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0;

-- Follow the chain to the head blocker (blocking_session_id = 0, but others point to it)
-- Then inspect what the head blocker is actually running:
SELECT text
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests r
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) t
WHERE r.session_id = @HeadBlockerSessionId;
commonMistakes: Treating any hanging query as a deadlock, when a true deadlock is auto-resolved within seconds, not left hanging
Killing the first blocked session found instead of tracing blocking_session_id to the actual head blocker
Killing a session without checking whether it's mid-write on a legitimate long-running job
Not distinguishing an application bug (an abandoned open transaction) from a genuinely busy, legitimate session
keyPoints: A hanging query with no error is ordinary blocking, not a deadlock -- deadlocks auto-resolve quickly
sys.dm_exec_requests' blocking_session_id column traces the blocking chain to the actual head blocker
Check what the head blocker is actually doing before killing it -- an abandoned transaction vs. a legitimate long write
Killing a session mid-write rolls back its work, which can be worse than waiting for it to finish

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes ordinary blocking from a deadlock
Correctly identifies how to find the head blocker (sys.dm_exec_requests / blocking_session_id)
Explains what to check before killing the blocking session
Provides correct, relevant diagnostic SQL

questions.title: A Covering Index Isn't Helping, and Nobody Knows Why
questions.prompt: A table has a nonclustered index covering exactly the columns a report query needs, but the query's execution plan still shows a full scan instead of using the index. The query is SELECT * FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail WHERE ProductID = 712. What's the most likely cause, and how would you fix the query?
questions.modelAnswer: SELECT * is almost certainly the cause. A covering index only helps when the query asks for columns the index actually includes; SELECT * asks for every column in the table, regardless of what's actually needed, which defeats the index's coverage the moment even one requested column isn't part of it. SQL Server then has to fall back to either a Key Lookup for each matching row or a full scan, depending on cost, instead of satisfying the query entirely from the narrower index. The fix is to name only the columns the report genuinely needs instead of SELECT *: SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty, UnitPrice FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail WHERE ProductID = 712. If those four columns are exactly what the covering index includes, the optimizer can now satisfy the entire query from the index alone, without ever touching the underlying table.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before touching the index, I'd actually look at the execution plan and the exact columns requested, because 'should use the index but doesn't' almost always traces back to the SELECT list, not the index definition. SELECT * is the first thing I'd check, because it's such a common habit and such a direct cause: if the index only covers four specific columns and the query asks for all fifteen columns on the table via *, the index simply can't satisfy that request on its own, and SQL Server has to go fetch the rest from the table itself — either via a Key Lookup per row or by abandoning the index entirely for a full scan, depending on how many rows are involved. The fix is almost always just naming the specific columns the report actually displays instead of *. I'd also double check that the index's included columns genuinely match what the report needs, because if even one required column is missing from the index, the same fallback happens no matter how narrowly I write the SELECT list.
commonMistakes: Assuming the index itself must be broken or missing, without checking what columns the query actually requests
Rebuilding or recreating the index before checking the SELECT list, missing the actual cause
Not verifying the index's included columns genuinely cover everything the trimmed SELECT list needs
Fixing this one query but not checking other queries against the same table for the identical SELECT * habit
keyPoints: SELECT * requests every column, defeating a covering index that only includes some of them
The fallback is a Key Lookup per row, or a full scan, instead of satisfying the query from the index alone
The fix is naming exactly the columns actually needed
The index's included columns must still genuinely match what's requested for this fix to work

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies SELECT * as the likely cause
Correctly explains why it defeats a covering index
Provides a correct fix naming specific columns
Notes the fix depends on the index already covering those exact columns

questions.title: A Merge That Tripled the Row Count
questions.prompt: After merging an orders DataFrame with a promotions DataFrame on promo_code, the result has three times as many rows as the original orders DataFrame. Diagnose what's causing this and how you'd fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: A merge multiplying row count is the signature of a many-to-many (or one-to-many on the wrong side) relationship on the join key: if promo_code isn't unique in the promotions DataFrame -- say, the same promo_code appears in three separate rows for three different date ranges or regions -- then every order matching that code gets duplicated once per matching promotion row, tripling the result for any order using a triple-duplicated code. The fix starts with actually checking: promotions['promo_code'].duplicated().sum() or promotions.groupby('promo_code').size() reveals whether the key is genuinely unique on that side. If it isn't supposed to be a one-to-many relationship, the real fix is deduplicating promotions down to one row per promo_code before merging (dropping duplicates, or aggregating down to the fields actually needed), rather than merging against a table that silently has multiple rows per key.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd check, before touching any code, is whether promo_code is actually unique in the promotions table -- promotions['promo_code'].value_counts() immediately tells me if some codes appear more than once. If a code appears three times, a merge on that key produces three matched rows for every order using it, which is exactly the tripling in the symptom described. This happens more often than people expect, because a promotions table might legitimately have multiple rows per code for different reasons -- different valid date ranges, different regions, a historical record of each time the promo was edited -- and merging against that table as if promo_code were a unique key silently fans out every matching order. Once I've confirmed that's the cause, the fix depends on what the merge was actually supposed to represent: if I only need the latest or currently-active promotion per code, I'd filter or deduplicate promotions down to one row per code before merging; if orders genuinely need to be linked to every matching promotion row for some other reason, then the row multiplication is actually correct behavior and the real bug is upstream, in expecting a 1:1 relationship that was never true.
questions.example:
# Diagnose: is promo_code actually unique on the promotions side?
print(promotions["promo_code"].duplicated().sum())
print(promotions.groupby("promo_code").size().sort_values(ascending=False).head())

# Fix: dedupe to the single row actually needed per code before merging
promotions_unique = promotions.sort_values("effective_date").drop_duplicates(
    "promo_code", keep="last"
)
merged = orders.merge(promotions_unique, on="promo_code", how="left")
commonMistakes: Assuming the join key is unique on both sides without actually checking
Fixing the symptom by dropping duplicate rows from the merged result instead of the actual duplicate keys from the source table
Not determining whether the fan-out is actually a bug or correct behavior for a genuine one-to-many relationship
Deduplicating promotions arbitrarily (e.g. keep='first') without checking which row is actually the correct one to keep
keyPoints: A merge multiplying row count signals a non-unique join key on at least one side
Checking value_counts()/duplicated() on the join key is the first diagnostic step
The fix is usually deduplicating the non-unique side before merging, keeping the intended row
Confirm whether the fan-out is actually incorrect before assuming it's a bug

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the non-unique join key as the cause
Describes a correct diagnostic check for key uniqueness
Provides a correct fix (deduplication before merging)
Considers whether the fan-out might be legitimate before fixing it

questions.title: Statistically Significant but Practically Meaningless
questions.prompt: An A/B test on 2 million users finds that the new homepage increases average time-on-page by 0.3 seconds, with p = 0.001. A stakeholder is excited and wants to ship it immediately as a major win. What would you point out before agreeing?
questions.modelAnswer: The core issue is conflating statistical significance with practical significance. With a sample as large as 2 million users, even a genuinely tiny, practically irrelevant effect will usually produce a very small p-value, because statistical power scales with sample size -- the test becomes extremely sensitive to detecting that a real difference exists at all, even if that difference is too small to matter. A p-value tells you whether an effect is probably real (not due to chance); it says nothing about whether the effect is big enough to care about. A 0.3-second increase in time-on-page is almost certainly too small to represent a meaningful behavioral or business change, regardless of how confidently the test detected it. Before agreeing this is a 'major win,' I'd ask what business outcome actually matters here (conversion rate, revenue, retention) and whether this change moves that outcome at all, and I'd present the actual effect size in context -- 0.3 seconds relative to a typical session length -- rather than letting the small p-value alone drive the celebration.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd gently separate two things that got merged together in how this is being presented: statistical significance and practical significance. At 2 million users, the test has enormous statistical power, which means it can detect genuinely tiny effects with high confidence -- that's actually exactly what a small p-value here is telling us, that the 0.3-second increase is probably real and not just noise. But 'probably real' and 'actually matters' are different questions, and 0.3 seconds of time-on-page is a vanishingly small effect in absolute terms. Before calling this a major win, I'd ask: does this change move any metric we actually care about, like conversion, revenue per user, or retention? If the only thing that moved is a fraction-of-a-second metric with no connection to a business outcome, I'd push back on the 'major win' framing specifically, not on whether to ship it -- shipping a harmless, statistically real but practically tiny change might still be fine, but it shouldn't be celebrated with the same enthusiasm as a change that actually moved something that matters to the business.
commonMistakes: Treating a very low p-value as automatically meaning the effect is important
Not connecting the result back to an actual business metric before calling it a win
Failing to explain why large sample sizes make tiny effects easy to detect statistically
Dismissing the result entirely instead of separating 'is it real' from 'does it matter'
keyPoints: Statistical significance means an effect is probably real; it says nothing about its size or importance
Very large sample sizes give tests the power to detect even trivially small effects
Practical significance requires connecting the effect to an actual business outcome
The right response distinguishes 'is this real' from 'does this matter,' not a flat yes/no on the result

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes statistical from practical significance
Correctly explains why large sample size produces small p-values for tiny effects
Proposes connecting the result to an actual business metric
Avoids simply dismissing the result outright

questions.title: A Bar Chart That's Technically Accurate but Misleading
questions.prompt: A colleague presents a bar chart with the y-axis starting at 90 instead of 0, showing conversion rate going from 91% to 94% across two quarters, and it looks like a dramatic jump. Every number on the chart is correct. What's the problem, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: The numbers being correct doesn't mean the chart is honest -- a truncated y-axis is one of the most common ways to mislead visually while staying technically accurate. Bar charts are read by comparing the relative heights of the bars, and that visual comparison implicitly assumes the axis starts at a meaningful baseline, usually zero. Starting the axis at 90 instead of 0 stretches a real 3-percentage-point change (91% to 94%, about a 3% relative increase) into bars that look roughly 3x different in height, visually suggesting a far more dramatic jump than actually occurred. The fix is to start the y-axis at 0 for a bar chart, which will correctly show two bars of very similar height for a genuinely small change -- if the change is actually meaningful but visually subtle at full scale, that's a presentation challenge to solve honestly (e.g., calling out the percentage-point change explicitly in a label or annotation), not a reason to truncate the axis to manufacture visual drama.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out that 'the numbers are correct' and 'the chart is honest' are two different claims, and this chart fails the second one even though it passes the first. Bar charts work by letting the eye compare bar heights, and that comparison only means what people assume it means if the axis starts at zero -- our brains read a bar twice as tall as meaning twice as much, and cutting the axis off at 90 breaks that assumption without telling the viewer. A 91% to 94% change is real, maybe three percentage points matters, but zooming the axis makes it look like a massive jump rather than the modest one it actually is. My fix is simple: redraw it with the y-axis starting at 0. If that makes the real change look visually subtle because it genuinely is subtle at full scale, that's not a flaw in the honest version of the chart -- it's accurate. If the change still deserves attention, I'd handle that with an explicit data label or annotation calling out '+3 points,' not by secretly stretching the axis to make a modest change look dramatic.
commonMistakes: Accepting the chart as fine because the underlying numbers are technically correct
Not recognizing a truncated axis specifically as a known, common way bar charts mislead
Fixing the chart by exaggerating further in the other direction rather than restoring an honest baseline
Not offering an alternative way to highlight a genuinely important small change (like a direct label) once the axis is corrected
keyPoints: Technical correctness of the numbers doesn't guarantee an honest visual impression
Bar chart height comparisons implicitly assume a zero baseline
A truncated y-axis exaggerates the visual magnitude of a real but modest change
The fix is a zero-based axis, with explicit labels/annotations if the modest change still needs emphasis

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the truncated y-axis as the specific problem
Explains why bar chart height comparisons assume a zero baseline
Proposes the correct fix (zero-based axis)
Offers an honest way to still emphasize a meaningful small change

lessonLink.label: Review: Misleading Charts & How to Avoid Them

questions.title: 99% Training Accuracy, 61% Test Accuracy
questions.prompt: A model you trained gets 99% accuracy on the training set but only 61% on the test set. Diagnose what's happening and describe at least three concrete things you'd try to fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: This gap is the classic signature of overfitting -- the model has learned the training data's specific noise and quirks rather than the general pattern, so it performs almost perfectly on data it's already seen and poorly on data it hasn't. To address it: (1) reduce model complexity -- for a tree-based model, limit max_depth or increase min_samples_leaf; for a linear model, add or strengthen regularization (L1/L2); (2) get more training data if feasible, since a more complex model needs more data to generalize rather than memorize; (3) use cross-validation during model selection instead of a single train/test split, to get a more reliable read on generalization performance while tuning; and (4) check for feature-level overfitting signals specifically, like an identifier-like feature (a row ID, a timestamp too close to the target) that the model could be exploiting to effectively memorize training rows rather than learning a real pattern.
questions.professionalAnswer: A 99-versus-61 gap is about as clear a sign of overfitting as you'll see -- the model has essentially memorized the training set rather than learning something that generalizes. My first move is usually to simplify the model: if it's a tree-based model, I'd cap max_depth or raise min_samples_leaf, because an unconstrained tree will happily keep splitting until it's basically memorized individual training rows. If it's a linear model, I'd add or strengthen L1/L2 regularization to penalize overly complex coefficient patterns. Second, I'd check whether there's a feature that's quietly letting the model cheat -- something like a row ID, a customer ID with no real predictive meaning, or a timestamp suspiciously close to the target event -- because models are very good at exploiting a leaky feature like that to get near-perfect training accuracy without learning anything real. Third, I'd move to proper cross-validation during model selection rather than tuning against a single train/test split, since that gives a steadier signal about actual generalization while I'm adjusting complexity. And if none of that closes the gap enough, I'd genuinely consider whether I just don't have enough training data for how complex this model is trying to be.
commonMistakes: Assuming the test set itself is just unlucky or unrepresentative rather than diagnosing overfitting
Only trying one fix (like adding more data) without addressing model complexity directly
Not checking for a leaky or identifier-like feature that could explain unnaturally high training accuracy
Tuning the model against the same single test set repeatedly, which risks overfitting to that set too
keyPoints: A large train/test accuracy gap is the classic overfitting signature
Reducing model complexity (depth limits, regularization) is a direct fix
A leaky or identifier-like feature can artificially inflate training accuracy
Cross-validation gives a more reliable generalization signal than a single split during tuning

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses overfitting as the cause
Proposes model-complexity reduction as a concrete fix
Proposes checking for leaky/identifier features
Proposes at least one additional valid fix (cross-validation, more data)

questions.title: A Model That's Suspiciously Perfect
questions.prompt: You build a churn prediction model and it achieves 99.8% accuracy on the test set almost immediately, with no tuning. Before celebrating, what would you suspect, and how would you investigate it?
questions.modelAnswer: A model that performs suspiciously well with almost no effort is a strong signal of data leakage -- information about the target variable has leaked into the features in a way that wouldn't be available at real prediction time. To investigate, I'd start by listing every feature and asking, for each one, 'would I actually have this value at the moment I need to make the prediction, before the outcome is known?' Common leakage culprits in a churn problem: a feature like cancellation_date_filled or last_login_days_ago computed using data from after the churn event itself, a feature that's a near-duplicate or derivative of the target (like a 'contract_still_active' flag that's almost the inverse of churn), or target leakage through an aggregated feature computed using the full dataset (including the test rows) rather than training data only. I'd also check feature importances -- if one single feature dominates with an importance far higher than everything else combined, that's often the leaking one, and removing it and re-running the model is a fast way to confirm the suspicion.
questions.professionalAnswer: 99.8% accuracy with zero tuning is a red flag, not a reason to celebrate -- in my experience, that level of 'too easy' almost always means leakage, not that I accidentally built an unusually good model on the first try. My first move is to check feature importances: if one feature is doing almost all the work, miles ahead of everything else, that's immediately suspicious, and I'd go look at exactly what that feature represents and when it would actually be known in a real prediction scenario. For a churn model specifically, I'm looking hard for anything computed from after the customer actually churned -- a 'days since last login' field that was calculated after they'd already left, a support-ticket count that spikes right before cancellation, or a field that's basically a disguised version of the label itself. I'd also check whether any feature was engineered using the full dataset, including the test rows, before the split happened -- that's a more subtle version of the same leakage. The real test is always: could I have known this feature's value at the actual moment I need to make the prediction, with the customer still active and the outcome still unknown? If the answer is no for any feature driving the result, that's the leak, and I'd remove it and rerun before trusting any of the model's numbers.
commonMistakes: Treating an unusually high accuracy as a success to report rather than a signal to investigate
Not checking feature importances to find which feature is suspiciously dominant
Missing leakage introduced by computing aggregated/derived features on the full dataset before splitting
Not applying the 'would this value actually be known at prediction time' test to every feature
keyPoints: Suspiciously perfect model performance is a leakage signal, not a win to report immediately
Checking feature importances for one dominant feature is a fast diagnostic
Features computed from after the outcome, or from the full dataset before splitting, are classic leakage sources
The 'would I know this at real prediction time' test should be applied to every feature

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly suspects data leakage rather than celebrating the result
Describes checking feature importances as a diagnostic step
Identifies concrete, realistic leakage sources for this scenario
Articulates the 'known at prediction time' test for each feature

questions.title: 98% Accuracy, Zero Fraud Caught
questions.prompt: A fraud-detection model reports 98% accuracy, but the team discovers it predicts 'not fraud' for every single transaction and still never catches an actual fraud case. Diagnose the root cause and describe how you'd fix both the evaluation approach and the model itself.
questions.modelAnswer: The root cause is severe class imbalance combined with the wrong evaluation metric: if only about 2% of transactions are actually fraud, a model that predicts 'not fraud' for everything achieves roughly 98% accuracy while having 0% recall on the class that actually matters. Accuracy is misleading here because it weighs the easy majority class (legitimate transactions) the same as the rare minority class (fraud), so a model can look great on accuracy while being completely useless at the actual task. The evaluation fix is to stop using accuracy as the primary metric for this problem and switch to precision, recall, F1, and a full confusion matrix -- especially recall on the fraud class, since missing fraud is the costly failure mode here. On the model side, options include: using class_weight='balanced' (or manually weighting) so the model is penalized more for misclassifying the rare class; resampling techniques like SMOTE (oversampling the minority class) or undersampling the majority class to rebalance what the model sees during training; and adjusting the classification threshold downward from the default 0.5 to make the model more willing to flag something as fraud, trading some precision for the recall that actually matters for this use case.
questions.professionalAnswer: The root cause is almost always the same story on an imbalanced problem: accuracy is a terrible primary metric when one class vastly outnumbers the other, because a model can get a great accuracy score just by always predicting the majority class and never actually doing the job. Here, if roughly 2% of transactions are fraud, 'always predict not-fraud' lands right around 98% accuracy while catching exactly zero real fraud -- which is precisely what happened. The first fix isn't to the model at all, it's to how we're measuring it: I'd throw out accuracy as the headline number and report precision, recall, and F1 specifically on the fraud class, plus the full confusion matrix, so everyone can see the zero-recall problem directly instead of it hiding behind a good-looking aggregate number. Once the evaluation is honest, the actual model fixes I'd try are: class_weight='balanced' so misclassifying a rare fraud case costs the model more during training than misclassifying a common legitimate transaction; resampling approaches like SMOTE to give the model more exposure to the minority class pattern during training; and lowering the decision threshold below the default 0.5, since the model might already be assigning fraud a higher probability than legitimate transactions on average, just never quite crossing 0.5 -- a lower threshold trades away some precision for the recall this specific business problem actually needs.
commonMistakes: Treating the 98% accuracy number as acceptable without checking the confusion matrix
Fixing only the model without first fixing the evaluation metric being used to judge it
Not recognizing that the default 0.5 classification threshold isn't appropriate for every business problem
Resampling the test set as well as the training set, which distorts the real-world evaluation
keyPoints: Severe class imbalance makes accuracy a misleading primary metric
Precision, recall, F1, and the confusion matrix reveal the zero-recall problem accuracy hides
class_weight='balanced' and resampling (SMOTE/undersampling) address the imbalance during training
Lowering the decision threshold is a direct lever to trade precision for recall on this class

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses class imbalance as the root cause
Correctly fixes the evaluation approach (metrics, confusion matrix)
Proposes concrete model-side fixes (class weighting, resampling)
Proposes threshold adjustment as an additional lever

questions.title: Cross-Validation Score Far Below Training Score
questions.prompt: A model scores 0.95 on training data but only 0.68 on 5-fold cross-validation, and the gap doesn't close no matter how much you tune hyperparameters. How would you use a learning curve to figure out what's actually going on, and what would each likely diagnosis mean for your next step?
questions.modelAnswer: A learning curve plots training and validation score against increasing amounts of training data, and it's the right diagnostic here because it distinguishes two very different problems that look similar from a single train/CV score comparison alone. If the training score stays high and the validation score rises steadily as more data is added but still hasn't converged with training score, that's a high-variance (overfitting) signature, and the direct fix is more training data if available, or reducing model complexity/adding regularization. If instead both curves plateau early and converge to each other at a mediocre score well below what's needed, that's a high-bias (underfitting) signature -- the model is too simple to capture the pattern even with ample data, and more data won't help; the fix is a more expressive model or better features, not more rows. Since hyperparameter tuning alone hasn't closed the gap in this scenario, the learning curve is specifically useful for telling you which of these two very different fixes is actually worth pursuing, rather than continuing to tune blindly.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before tuning anything further, I'd plot a learning curve, because 'training score much higher than CV score' can mean two genuinely different things, and I want to know which one I'm dealing with before spending more time. The learning curve plots both training and validation score as a function of how much training data the model actually sees. If I see the validation score still climbing as I add more data, with the gap between training and validation narrowing but not yet closed, that tells me this is primarily a variance problem -- the model would likely keep improving with more data, or I could speed that up by simplifying the model or adding regularization right now. If instead both curves flatten out early and converge to roughly the same mediocre score, that's a bias problem -- the model has essentially hit a ceiling regardless of how much data it sees, which means more data won't fix anything; what's needed is a fundamentally more expressive model or better features that actually capture the signal. The reason I lean on this specific diagnostic rather than just continuing to tune hyperparameters is that hyperparameter tuning mostly helps with the variance side of this -- if the real problem is bias, no amount of regularization tweaking will close that gap, and the learning curve is what tells me to stop wasting time there and go get better features instead.
commonMistakes: Continuing to tune hyperparameters indefinitely without diagnosing whether the real problem is bias or variance
Assuming more training data always helps, even when the learning curve shows a bias (plateaued) pattern
Misreading a learning curve by not looking at whether the curves are still converging or have already flattened
Not distinguishing that hyperparameter tuning mainly addresses variance, not bias
keyPoints: A learning curve plots train/validation score against training set size
Still-converging curves with a shrinking gap indicate a variance (overfitting) problem, fixable with more data or regularization
Early-plateauing, converged curves at a low score indicate a bias (underfitting) problem, not fixable with more data
Hyperparameter tuning mainly helps variance; a bias problem needs a more expressive model or better features

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes how a learning curve is constructed and read
Correctly diagnoses the high-variance pattern and its fix
Correctly diagnoses the high-bias pattern and its fix
Explains why hyperparameter tuning alone wouldn't fix a bias problem

questions.title: Choosing a clustering key for a new fact-staging table
questions.prompt: You're designing a new staging table that will be loaded nightly and queried immediately afterward by ProductID ranges. A table can have only one clustered index. Explain the difference between a clustered and nonclustered index, and what makes a good choice of clustering key.
questions.modelAnswer: A clustered index determines the actual physical order rows are stored in on disk -- which is exactly why a table can have only one: data can only be physically sorted one way. A nonclustered index is a separate structure that holds a sorted copy of the indexed column(s) plus a pointer back to the actual row, and a table can have many of them. Looking up a row through the clustering key is fastest, since SQL Server navigates directly to the physical location; looking up through a nonclustered index takes one extra step -- find the index entry, then follow the pointer back to the row. A good clustering key is narrow (a small data type, since every nonclustered index secretly stores the clustering key as its row pointer), unique (no ambiguity about physical order), and ever-increasing (so new rows append at the end instead of forcing existing rows to physically shuffle). Given the staging table is loaded nightly and then range-queried by ProductID, an ever-increasing identity key for the clustered index, with a nonclustered index on ProductID to support the range queries, is the more defensible design than clustering directly on ProductID.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this as two separate decisions. First: what should the table's physical row order be -- that's the clustered index, and I only get one shot at it. Second: what other lookup patterns do I need to support cheaply -- that's where nonclustered indexes come in, and I can have several. For a staging table that's loaded nightly, I actually lean toward an ever-increasing identity column as the clustering key rather than ProductID directly, even though ProductID is the column people will query by. The reason is load performance: an ever-increasing key means new rows always append at the end of the physical order, so the nightly load doesn't cause page splits from inserting into the middle of existing data. Then I add a nonclustered index on ProductID to support the range queries -- yes, that costs one extra pointer-following step per lookup compared to clustering directly on ProductID, but it's a much smaller cost than the load-time page-splitting I'd get from clustering on a column that isn't naturally ordered or unique.
commonMistakes: Assuming more indexes are always better without considering the nightly load's insert cost
Choosing a wide, non-unique column as the clustering key, which bloats every nonclustered index that secretly carries it as a pointer
Forgetting a table can have only one clustered index, and trying to 'cluster' on two different columns
Not connecting the ever-increasing key recommendation to the specific nightly-load write pattern described in the scenario
keyPoints: Clustered index = physical row order, one per table
Nonclustered index = separate structure with a pointer back to the row, many allowed
Good clustering key: narrow, unique, ever-increasing
Design choice should weigh load (insert) pattern against query (read) pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the clustered vs. nonclustered distinction
Correctly lists the three traits of a good clustering key
Applies the tradeoff to the specific nightly-load scenario given
Recommends a nonclustered index to support the ProductID range queries

questions.title: Designing an A/B Test Before Writing Any Analysis Code
questions.prompt: Product wants to know if a new onboarding flow improves 7-day retention. Before writing any analysis code, walk through the key design decisions you'd make for this A/B test: the metric, sample size considerations, randomization unit, and how long to run it.
questions.modelAnswer: First, I'd pin down the primary metric precisely before anything else: '7-day retention' needs an exact, unambiguous definition (e.g., did the user open the app at least once between day 2 and day 7 after signup) agreed on upfront, so there's no room to redefine it after seeing favorable results. Second, randomization unit: users should be randomized at signup, one time, into control (old flow) or treatment (new flow) -- not re-randomized per session, which would contaminate the comparison by exposing the same user to both experiences. Third, sample size: I'd run a power analysis before launching, using the current baseline retention rate, the smallest effect size that would actually be worth caring about (the minimum detectable effect), and a standard significance level and power (commonly alpha=0.05, power=0.80) to calculate how many users per arm are needed -- launching without this risks either running far longer than necessary or stopping too early with an underpowered, inconclusive result. Fourth, duration: the test needs to run long enough to actually observe the full 7-day retention window for every user enrolled, plus ideally spanning at least one full weekly cycle to avoid day-of-week effects, and it shouldn't be stopped early just because an interim peek looks favorable, since repeated early peeking inflates the false-positive rate.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd work through this in a specific order, because getting the order wrong is how experiments go sideways. First, I nail down exactly what '7-day retention' means in measurable terms and write it down before anyone sees a single result -- otherwise there's a real risk of quietly redefining the metric later if the obvious definition doesn't show the result someone wants. Second, randomization has to happen once per user, at signup, not per session -- if the same user could land in both groups across different sessions, the comparison is contaminated and I can't trust it. Third, and this is the step I see skipped most often: before launching anything, I'd run a sample size / power calculation using the current baseline retention rate and the smallest improvement that would actually be worth shipping for. Skipping this means either the test runs way longer than it needs to, burning time, or it gets called early with too few users to actually detect anything reliably. Fourth, duration: the test needs to run long enough that every enrolled user has actually had their full 7 days to either retain or not, and I'd want it to span at least a full week of calendar time so day-of-week patterns in signup behavior don't skew the comparison. And I'd set the stopping rule in advance too -- no peeking at interim results and calling it early just because day 3 looks good, because that kind of early stopping is a well-known way to inflate false positives.
commonMistakes: Starting to analyze results before precisely defining the metric in measurable terms
Randomizing per session instead of per user, contaminating the comparison
Skipping a sample size / power calculation before launching the test
Stopping the test early based on favorable interim results, inflating the false-positive rate
keyPoints: The metric must be defined precisely and in advance, before any results are seen
Randomization should happen once per user, not per session
A sample-size/power calculation should be done before launch, not after
The test must run long enough to observe the full metric window and avoid early-stopping bias

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly addresses precise metric definition upfront
Correctly addresses the randomization unit (per user, not per session)
Correctly addresses sample size / power considerations before launch
Correctly addresses test duration and the risk of early stopping

questions.title: Wide Format or Long Format for a Reporting Dataset?
questions.prompt: You're preparing a dataset of monthly sales by region for both a downstream statistical analysis in Python and a dashboard tool. One format puts each month in its own column (wide); the other puts month as a single column with a value column (long/tidy). Walk through how you'd decide which structure to design the dataset around.
questions.modelAnswer: The decision hinges on what the data will actually be used for downstream, not personal preference. Long (tidy) format -- one row per region-month-value combination -- is generally the better default for analysis: most statistical functions, groupby operations, and plotting libraries (including matplotlib/seaborn in Python, and most BI tools) expect one observation per row, and long format scales naturally if a new month or region is added, since it just means more rows, not more columns. Wide format -- one row per region with a column per month -- is sometimes more convenient for direct human reading (a small table someone scans visually) or for certain matrix-style operations like correlation between specific months. Since the question states this feeds both a Python statistical analysis and a dashboard tool, I'd design the canonical stored dataset in long format, since that's what both pandas and most dashboard tools can reshape from easily (pivoting wide for display is a cheap, one-line operation from long data), whereas going the other direction -- un-pivoting a wide table back to long for analysis -- is more error-prone and a step that has to be repeated for every downstream consumer.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd anchor this decision in the downstream consumers rather than defaulting to whichever format looks nicer in a spreadsheet. Long format -- region, month, sales_value, one row per combination -- is what pandas groupby, most plotting libraries, and most statistical functions actually expect to operate on; it's also the format that handles a growing dataset gracefully, since adding a new month just means appending rows, not restructuring columns. Wide format, with a column per month, reads nicer to a human scanning a small table by eye, and it's occasionally handy for specific matrix operations, but it gets awkward fast as more months accumulate, and most analysis code ends up reshaping it back to long anyway before doing anything useful with it. Given that this dataset explicitly needs to feed both a Python analysis and a dashboard tool, I'd store the canonical version in long format and treat 'wide' as a presentation-time transformation, not the storage format -- pivoting long data to wide for a specific chart or table is one line of code (pivot_table or pivot in pandas, or the dashboard tool's own pivot feature), while repeatedly un-pivoting wide data back to long for every new analysis is the more fragile, repeated-effort direction to design around.
commonMistakes: Choosing wide format by default because it's easier to read by eye in a spreadsheet
Not considering that most Python analysis and plotting tools expect long/tidy data
Designing the stored format around one specific downstream use (the dashboard) without considering the other (the analysis)
Not recognizing that pivoting long to wide is cheap, while un-pivoting wide to long repeatedly is more error-prone
keyPoints: Long (tidy) format -- one row per observation -- is the better default for most analysis tooling
Wide format is more convenient for direct human reading or certain matrix operations
The decision should be driven by downstream consumers, not visual preference
Pivoting long data to wide for presentation is cheaper than repeatedly un-pivoting wide data for analysis

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the difference between wide and long format
Correctly reasons about tooling compatibility (pandas, plotting, dashboards)
Makes a clear, justified recommendation grounded in the stated use case
Notes the asymmetry between pivoting and un-pivoting effort

questions.title: Designing the Train/Validation/Test Split for Time-Series Data
questions.prompt: You're building a model to predict next-month customer churn using historical monthly snapshots. A junior teammate suggests a random 70/15/15 train/validation/test split, the same way they'd split an i.i.d. dataset. Explain what's wrong with that approach here and design the split you'd actually use.
questions.modelAnswer: A random split assumes the rows are independent and identically distributed, which isn't true for time-ordered monthly snapshots -- a random split would scatter months from the same time period across train, validation, and test, letting the model effectively 'see the future' relative to some of its own training data (for example, training on March and May data while validating on April). That's a leakage problem specific to temporal data: the model could learn patterns that happen to hold in that mixed-up arrangement but wouldn't actually be available at real prediction time, where you only ever have the past to predict the future. The correct design is a chronological split: train on the earliest block of months, validate on the next block forward in time, and test on the most recent block, so every evaluation is strictly made on data that comes after everything the model was trained on -- mimicking exactly how the model will actually be used in production, where it only ever predicts forward from what's already happened.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on the random split specifically because the data isn't i.i.d. -- it's time-ordered, and that changes the rules. A random 70/15/15 split would happily put March data in the training set and February data in the test set, which means the model could be evaluated on 'predicting' something chronologically earlier than data it already trained on. That's not how this model will actually be used in production -- it will only ever have the past available to predict forward -- so testing it any other way gives a misleadingly optimistic result that won't hold up once it's actually deployed. What I'd design instead is a strictly chronological split: the earliest span of months becomes the training set, the next span forward in time becomes validation, and the most recent span becomes the test set, with no reshuffling across that boundary.
